messages.subject: Re: labeling boxplots
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's an example from a post by Dr. Bryan Hanson earlier this summer; perhaps it can help you in your problem. It doesn't provide a direct solution, but elements of the code may give you some avenues to pursue.

HTH,
Dennis

# test data
res = c(rnorm(10, 5, 1.5), rnorm(10, 8, 2), rnorm(10, 14, 2.0),
        rnorm(10, 10, 1.5), rnorm(10, 15, 2), rnorm(10, 12,2.5))
fac1 <- c(rep("L", 20), rep("M", 20), rep("H", 20))
fac1 <- factor(fac1, levels = c("L", "M", "H"))
fac2 <- c(rep("WT", 10), rep("GM", 10))
fac2 <- as.factor(rep(fac2, 3))
td <- data.frame(r = res, f1 = fac1, f2 = fac2)
td[c(13,32:33, 55:58), 1] <- NA
td <- na.omit(td)

ggplot(td, aes(x = f1, y = r, colour = f2, group = f2)) +
   stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "line") +
   geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.05)) +
   stat_bin(aes(x = f1, y = c(-0.5, 0.8)[as.numeric(f2)],
     label=paste("n =", ..count..)), geom = "text", legend = FALSE) +
   scale_colour_manual(name = "", values = c('red', 'blue'))

messages.subject: Re: labeling boxplots
messages.body_plain:
It just requires a little playing around. See below.

On Thu, Sep 30, 2010 at 11:38 PM, jacktanner <ih...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> Ista, that's a great suggestion. That method works for the mtcars
> data, but it doesn't work in a more complicated case:
>
> mydf=data.frame(list(
>  f1=factor(rep(c("a","b"), each=15)),
>  f2=factor(rep(c("x","y","z"), each=5)),
>  y=as.vector(sapply(1:6, function(x) { rnorm(5, x, 1) }))
> ))
>
>> mydf.size <- ddply(mydf, .(f1, f2), summarise, y=mean(y), n=length(y))
>> p = ggplot(mydf) + geom_boxplot(aes(x=f1, y=y, fill=f2))
>> p + geom_text(aes(label=paste("n =", n)), data=mydf.size)
>
> Error in which(cat) : argument to 'which' is not logical
>

One thing I notice about this is that geom_text might not know what
any of it's aesthetics are, because none are specified in the ggplot
call or in the geom_text call. So move the x, y, and fill
specification out of the geom_boxplot call and into the ggplot call:

p <- ggplot(mydf, aes(x=f1, y=y, fill=f2)) + geom_boxplot()
p + geom_text(aes(label=paste("n =", n), group = f2), data=mydf.size)

that almost worked except that the text labels were stacked instead of
dodged. So I tried

p + geom_text(aes(label=paste("n =", n), group = f2), data=mydf.size,
position=position_dodge(width=.75))

and that seems to work (the width=.75 was arrived at by trial and error).

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: ..density.. in stat_bin for categorical data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kohske,

That patch would fix the bug, but I'm not sure using a density with
discrete data really makes sense.

Hadley

On Mon, Sep 27, 2010 at 11:07 AM, takahashi kohske
<takahash...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi list members,
>
> I want to know if this behavior is planned.
>
> When I draw the bar of rate of each category for total count,
>
> d<-data.frame(x=gl(2,10)) # the rates are 0.5 for category 1 and 0.5
> for category 2
> ggplot(d,aes(x,group=1))+stat_bin(aes(y=..density..))
>
> For categorical data, the density of each bar exceed 0.5.
> It is because width of the bar is 0.9 by default,
> but for categorical data, the width of the bar has no meaning more
> than just appearance, unlike for continuous variable.
>
> if I specify the width explicitly, the density is correctly calculated:
>
> ggplot(d,aes(x,group=1))+stat_bin(aes(y=..density..),width=1)
>
> but in this case, there is no space between the bars.
>
> So, for categorical data, should the parameter `width' have no effect
> on the calculation?
> Here I put the example of modification:
>
> StatBin$calculate<-function(., data, scales, binwidth=NULL,
> origin=NULL, breaks=NULL, width=0.9, drop = FALSE, right = TRUE, ...)
> {
>    range <- scales$x$output_set()
>
>    if (is.null(breaks) && is.null(binwidth) && !is.integer(data$x) &&
> !.$informed) {
>      message("stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth
> = x' to adjust this.")
>      .$informed <- TRUE
>    }
>
>        w<-if(is.integer(data$x))1 else width  # use 1 instead of width in
> calculating bins for categorical data
>    r<-bin(data$x, data$weight, binwidth=binwidth, origin=origin,
> breaks=breaks, range=range, width=w, drop = drop, right = right)
>    r$width<-width # width should control the appearance of the bar.
>
>    return(r)
>  }
>
>
> thanks,
>
> kohske
>

messages.subject: Re: ..density.. in stat_bin for categorical data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley

I agree. Probably using a density for categorical data does not make sense.
We should use the number (frequency) of each category instead of the
relative frequency (i.e., density), because a part of information will
be lost by using relative frequency.
But in some case, we use the relative frequency (or percentage of each
category), perhaps for the purpose of simplification...

anyway, thanks a lot.

kohske

Thanks

The problem with interp is something I have also encountered with
ggplot2. This is because ggplot2 exports all functions, even local
ones.. If another package has a function or method of the same name it
will be masked if you load ggplot after the other package, The
solution is for ggplot to use the namespace to export only those
methods that the user needs to see.

What I haven´t worked out how to do is to get ggplot2 to do the
interpolation so that I don´t have to use akima::interp at all. Also
is it possible to specify what contour lines to draw? The default is
uniformily spaced bins but what if you are plotting a likelihood
surface and want to draw the probability levels corresponding to 0.9,
0.99 and 0.999?

Laurie

 geom_contour(aes(x=X1,y=X2,z=z),breaks=c(0,.5,.70,1))+

 scale_fill_manual(values=c("red","yellow","green"),

Jonathan

Should be able to do it just by having a stat_smooth() for each set of Y data.

c <- ggplot(datax, aes(x=Distance))

stat_smooth(aes(y=Signal1), fill=”darkgrey”, colour=”red”, size=2, alpha = 0.2)+
stat_smooth(aes(y=Signal2), fill=”grey80”, colour=”blue”, size=2, alpha = 0.2)

If it starts to get too complex consider using reshape/melt.

datax2 <- melt(datax, id.vars=Distance)

d <- ggplot(datax, aes(x=Distance, y=value))

d + stat_smooth(aes(colour = variable), size = 2, alpha = 0.2)

messages.subject: Re: Frequency histogram
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Not that I endorse this type of histogram as a general rule, but perhaps this would be suitable:

dat2 <- dat    # copy original df as a backup
# Alter some values in the 500-800 category - idea is to copy it twice for three copies,
# divide the total frequency by 3 in these replicate categories and remove the
# text except for the middle one of the replicated categories
dat[7:8, ] <- dat[6, ]          # replicate last row twice
dat[6:8, 2] <- 5                 # divide frequency by 3 in each of these categories
dat[7:8, 3] <- c(7, 8)        # replace frequency.n
dat$endurance <- as.character(dat$endurance)   # change first var to character
dat[c(6, 8), 1] <- ""          # blank out text in edges of the three replicated categories
dat
  endurance lamps endurance.n
1   0 - 100    82           1
2 100 - 200    71           2
3 200 - 300    68           3
4 300 - 400    56           4
5 400 - 500    43           5
6               5           6
7 500 - 800     5           7
8               5           8
str(dat)
'data.frame':   8 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ endurance  : chr  "0 - 100" "100 - 200" "200 - 300" "300 - 400" ...
 $ lamps      : num  82 71 68 56 43 5 5 5
 $ endurance.n: num  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

# Subtract 0.5 from the breaks to center the labels

ggplot(dat, aes(x=endurance.n)) +
   geom_histogram(aes(weight=lamps), binwidth=1) +

   scale_x_continuous(breaks=dat$endurance.n - 0.5, labels=dat$endurance)

Normally, you'd want a color aesthetic to demarcate the categories, but not
in this case because you're using three categories to represent one long one.
The frequencies are divided by three in each constructed subcategory
in order to maintain the correct area.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Following this post, I can plot an image as background :)
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/beff7d92f05dc741

and height to 1npc. However, this does not allow to zoom on certain
parts of the plot. I am wondering whether there is a way to write an
enhanced background function that would
 - display the pixmap following the x and y scales if they are
specified,
 - set the scales to the pixmap size if they are not specified.

As I am not very familiar with the engine behind ggplot2, I would
appreciate any comment on whether this is doable or not? If yes, how
would you access the x and y limits (as it looks like they are
computed on display time)?

Thank you in advance for your help,

Thomas

messages.subject_clean: OT: Description of facet chart in text
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this is somewhat off topic but I was wondering how you guys are
normally handling it.
I stay away from facets but every now and then I use them. In latex I
include it via a figure, giving me one label/caption. And now I am
wondering how you normally describe a facet (ie. 3x2) in the free
flowing text? None of the 'rectangle boxes' in the chart (at least
when produced with ggplot2) have a specific ID, so how are you
referencing it? "When Headline A and Headline B are this and that"?

Thanks in advance.

Best,
Thomas

The code you gave didn't run as written, and had some other problems
as well.  But I was able to get to what I think your problem is.  I'm
going to set aside that you seem like you are trying to make a
"dynamite plot" (http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/twiki/pub/Main/
TatsukiRcode/Poster3.pdf) and focus on the error.

A minimized example:

DF <- structure(list(name = structure(c(2L, 1L), .Label = c("C", "D"
), class = "factor"), total = c(1, 2.02961986153729)), .Names =
c("name",
"total"), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

ggplot() +
 layer(data=DF, mapping=aes(x=name,y=total), geom="bar",
stat="identity") +
coord_trans(y = "log10")
# Error in if (length(from) == 1 || length(to) == 1 || from[1] ==
from[2] ||  :
#  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

ggplot() +
 layer(data=DF, mapping=aes(x=name,y=total), geom="bar",
stat="identity") +
scale_y_log10()
# produces a plot without error or warning

I am also surprised that these behave differently, but I would expect
both to not work.  If you look at the un-transformed version:

ggplot() +
 layer(data=DF, mapping=aes(x=name,y=total), geom="bar",
stat="identity")

you have a regular bar plot with the y-axis ranging from 0 to 2.  If I
log10 transform these two points, I get -Inf, 0.3.  Bar plots start at
0, and 0 on a log scale is minus infinity; bar plots and log scale
axes are inherently incompatible. (Granted, deducing that from the
error message given would take working through details of the source
code.)  I would recommend looking at the pointrange geom.

DF <- structure(list(name = structure(c(4L, 3L, 3L, 1L, 2L), .Label =
c("xxx",
"xxx xxxxxx", "xxx xxxxxx (xx xxxxxxx)", "xxxxxx"), class =
"factor"),

    1010.038, 8754.674), median = c(0, 0.5, 383, 441, 7595.5),
    total.h = c(1.00041195196771, 2.0302456440019, 9.46857659298375,
    12.8099557850261, 111.020044365812), total.l =
c(0.999588048032286,
    2.02899407907269, 9.46419545073598, 12.8040730740514,
110.993852624018
    ), type = c(2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L)), .Names = c("name", "total",
"mad", "mean", "median", "total.h", "total.l", "type"), class =
"data.frame", row.names = c("1",
"2", "3", "4", "5"))

ggplot() +
 layer(data=DF,
mapping=aes(x=factor(name),y=total,ymin=total.l,ymax=total.h),geom="pointrange")

+
coord_trans(y = "log10")

ggplot() +
 layer(data=DF,
mapping=aes(x=factor(name),y=total,ymin=total.l,ymax=total.h),
geom="pointrange") +
scale_y_log10()

On Tue, Oct 5, 2010 at 9:17 AM, Manuel Spínola <mspin...@gmail.com> wrote:

Yes, but...a plot of what? Predictions, residuals (which type?) or partial residuals are all possibilities for the vertical axis.

Perhaps you want something analogous to termplot() in base graphics, which can be applied to both lm() and glm() fitted objects. One possibility is to return the information you need into a data frame, e.g.,  res   x1   x2   x3   x4 (obtained from a glm model fit), melt it using res as the id variable and then use facet_wrap() in conjunction with ggplot() + ...  to get the final product. With facet_wrap(),  you should be able to get smooths for each variable individually. This would be consistent with Hadley's advice.

I'm reposting this to the list because others may have useful advice on this front, particularly those who have extensive experience with logistic regression. My inclination would be to plot appropriate forms of residuals by covariate - is there a useful context in which predicted values by covariate makes sense in logistic models?

messages.subject: Efficent way of creating a contour
messages.subject_clean: Efficent way of creating a contour
messages.body_plain:
All,

I have been working on a constrained optimization problem where I find the solution graphically (think Lagrange multipliers).  The idea is I want to find the number of items (n) and the number of measurements per item (m) that minimizes some cost function subject to the constraint that the estimation precision of a function of interest (a standard error) is less than a certain value.  So the idea behind the plot is to have a contour that shows the contours of the cost function, the contours of the standard error, and a region that is not allowed since these values of (n,m) do not satisfy the constraint.  My professor wants me to "cross hatch out" the region that is not allowed.  Attached to this email is one of these plots so that you can better understand my description.  The dashed lines represent the contours for the standard error and the thick solid contours represent the cost function.  Also the asterisk is the optimum point.  I can do this plot by hand, but, one plot takes around 1-2 hours to create.  My question is is anyone familiar of a quicker way of doing this?  Currently the way I do it is create the contours and then add a geom_line for each individual line in the cross hatch region.  My code is below and I am attaching a data set that was used to create the plot.  I thank you all for your help ahead of time.

Brian

library(ggplot2)

dat <- read.table("your directory here...constrained_optim.txt",header = T)

#Selecting the values that satisfy the constraint and saving as a separate object
t.id <http://t.id> <- which(dat$SE <= 0.8)
xx <- dat[t.id <http://t.id>,]
tt <- which(xx[,3] == min(xx[,3]))
xx[tt,]  ##Solution to optimum problem

##Creating the plot object
v <- ggplot(dat,aes(x = n, y = m, z = cost))
p <- v + geom_contour(breaks = seq(48600,80000,by = 7500),size = 1 ,color = "black" )+
stat_contour(data = dat,aes(x = n,y = m, z = SE),
             lty = 2, breaks = c(0.7906603,0.75,0.7)) +
geom_point(aes(x = dat$n, y = dat$m), size =0) +
geom_point(aes(x = xx[tt,1],y = xx[tt,2]),shape = 8,size = 4)+theme_bw() +
ylab("Number of Measurements (m)") + xlab("Number of Units (n)")+
geom_text(aes(x = 11.3, y = 20),label = 49,angle = 45, size = 4, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 13.8, y = 20),label = 56,angle = 45, size = 4, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 16.3, y = 20),label = 64,angle = 45, size = 4, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 18.7, y = 20),label = 71,angle = 45, size = 4, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 20, y = 4.4),label = 0.79, size = 3, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 20, y = 5.6),label = 0.75, size = 3, hjust = 0)+
geom_text(aes(x = 20, y = 8.8),label = 0.7, size =3, hjust = 0)
p

#Now adding the cross hatch region
pp <- p+geom_line(aes(x = c(19,20),y = c(3,4)) )+
geom_line(aes(x = c(18,19.5),y = c(3,4.6)) )+

On Tue, Oct 5, 2010 at 20:23, Brian Weaver <the...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> All,
>
> I have been working on a constrained optimization problem where I find the solution graphically (think Lagrange multipliers).  The idea is I want to find the number of items (n) and the number of measurements per item (m) that minimizes some cost function subject to the constraint that the estimation precision of a function of interest (a standard error) is less than a certain value.  So the idea behind the plot is to have a contour that shows the contours of the cost function, the contours of the standard error, and a region that is not allowed since these values of (n,m) do not satisfy the constraint.  My professor wants me to "cross hatch out" the region that is not allowed.  Attached to this email is one of these plots so that you can better understand my description.  The dashed lines represent the contours for the standard error and the thick solid contours represent the cost function.  Also the asterisk is the optimum point.  I can do this plot by hand, but, one plot takes around 1-2 hours to create.  My question is is anyone familiar of a quicker way of doing this?  Currently the way I do it is create the contours and then add a geom_line for each individual line in the cross hatch region.  My code is below and I am attaching a data set that was used to create the plot.  I thank you all for your help ahead of time.

> HI:
>
> On Tue, Oct 5, 2010 at 9:17 AM, Manuel Spínola <mspin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thank you very much Dennis.
> >
> > Suppose that I have 4 covariates
> >
> > model = glm(response ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family=binomail(logit), data = mydata)
> >
> > Now I would like a plot for each covariate but according to the fitted model using stat_smooth, so I need to select one variable at the time, but how I do this using stat_smooth?
>
> Yes, but...a plot of what? Predictions, residuals (which type?) or partial residuals are all possibilities for the vertical axis.
>
> Perhaps you want something analogous to termplot() in base graphics, which can be applied to both lm() and glm() fitted objects. One possibility is to return the information you need into a data frame, e.g.,  res   x1   x2   x3   x4 (obtained from a glm model fit), melt it using res as the id variable and then use facet_wrap() in conjunction with ggplot() + ...  to get the final product. With facet_wrap(),  you should be able to get smooths for each variable individually. This would be consistent with Hadley's advice.
>
> I'm reposting this to the list because others may have useful advice on this front, particularly those who have extensive experience with logistic regression. My inclination would be to plot appropriate forms of residuals by covariate - is there a useful context in which predicted values by covariate makes sense in logistic models?
>
> Dennis
>
> > The example in stat_smooth for logistic regression appear to be for a simple model (only 1 covariate), right?
> > Best,
> >
> > Manuel
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On 05/10/2010 09:45 a.m., Dennis Murphy wrote:

Hadley,

I think I saw that you said something similar on a Nabble or LearnR blog or something. The only issue is that I have ordered my Varieties in a very particularly way so that each type is a row (can you order a character list?).  As far as I know, this means that Variety has to be a factor, which means that when I subset it (and keep the correct order of things) that I'm subsetting a factor and the extra labels are retained.

Am I just being lazy? I swear I'm not trying to be. I just want something that will let me show some beautiful graphs to my boss so he's happy, with as little fuss as possible.

Speaking of which... is this it?

droplevels <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("droplevels")

droplevels.factor <- function(x, ...) factor(x)

droplevels.data.frame <- function(x, except = NULL, ...)

  {

    ix <- sapply(x, is.factor)

    if (!is.null(except)) ix[except] <- FALSE

    x[ix] <- lapply(x[ix], factor)

    x

  }

I think it works...

Brandon

build and it worked great with the usage that Takahashi suggested. R

droplevels <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("droplevels")

  {
    ix <- sapply(x, is.factor)
    if (!is.null(except)) ix[except] <- FALSE
    x[ix] <- lapply(x[ix], factor)
    x
  }

Thomas,

The default colour is NA according to Hadley's page.
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_polygon.html

This means that the border between area's won't be shown so selecting
a linetype won't make a difference because it won't be shown. After
playing, it seems that when you define a colour you see the line, but
then linetype fails to work because you've defined a colour.

There's probably a workaround, but I don't see it.

Brandon

hi, probably this is a bug.
put this code before using goem_polygon

GeomPolygon$draw<- function (., data, scales, coordinates, ...)
{
    n <- nrow(data)
    if (n == 1)
        return()
    ggname(.$my_name(), gTree(children = gList(with(coordinates$munch(data,
        scales), polygonGrob(x, y, default.units = "native",
        gp = gpar(col = colour, fill = alpha(fill, alpha), lwd = size *
            .pt, lty = linetype))))))
}

to Hadley:
the argument in gar in polygonGrob in gTree in ggname, linetype =
linetype should be lty = linetype.
as far as i inspected, this appears only in GeomPolygon$draw but not
in other goems.

messages.subject: Re: different legends
messages.body_plain:
If you want all of your legend labels in italics you can use legend.text in the options.

http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Legend-Attributes

/shameless self-promotion

#usage
plot + opts(legend.text = theme_text(face = 'italic'))

It's really hard to make out what you mean by two legends though. Usually if there are two legends it's because you have defined two separate scales (color, shape, size, linetype...). You can make them disappear, but I'm not sure if you can just combine legends.

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Is this perhaps (close to) what you wanted?

p1<-ggplot(tab,aes(ct,ccb,colour=espécie,shape=sexo))
q1 <- p1 + geom_point(size=2.5) + scale_shape("Sexo") +
     labs(x="Comprimento padrão (cm)", y="Comprimento côndilo-basal (mm)") +
     opts(legend.position="none")
p3 <- ggplot(tab, aes(ccb, lr, colour=espécie, shape=sexo))
q2 <- p3 + geom_point(size=2.5) + scale_shape("Sexo") +
     labs(x="Comprimento côndilo-basal (mm)",y="Largura rostral (mm)") +
     opts(legend.text=theme_text(face ="italic"))

grid.newpage()
vp1 <- viewport(width = 0.4, height = 1, x = 0.2, y = 0.5)
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.6, height = 1, x = 0.7, y = 0.5)
print(q1, vp = vp1)
print(q2, vp = vp2)

The page rendering uses the grid package; the code is a modification of the examples in section 8.4 of Hadley's book. The warnings will tell you that the observations with missing values are deleted from the plot.

It's not obvious to me how one would do it since the font family cannot be set within scale_*. (But I'd be interested to see how it's done if they indeed can have separate fonts :) You could try to separate the two legends - the shapes with one plot and the species with the other, but I had some problems getting that to work and don't have the time to play with it. If you do that, however, you're basically stealing space from the plots to devote to the legends and you have to ask yourself if it's worth the trouble.

Hi:

Thanks to Luciano and Ista for pointing me in the right direction - I had done some searching of the list archives but hadn't found what I needed. The following replacement seems to work for the q2 plot:

q2 <- p3 + geom_point(size=2.5) + scale_shape("Sexo") +
     labs(x="Comprimento côndilo-basal (mm)",y="Largura rostral (mm)") +

     scale_colour_hue(breaks = levels(espécie),
              labels=parse(text=c(paste('italic("',unique(espécie)[1:2],'")'))))

Substitute this into my earlier script and hopefully that gets what Daniele wanted.

Dennis

messages.subject: Setting xlim() with geom_area *increases* the range of the y axis (sometimes significantly)
messages.subject_clean: Setting xlim() with geom_area *increases* the range of the y axis (sometimes significantly)
messages.body_plain:
ggplot2 is super nice. I'm hoping the following is simply me being
confused.

Appending xlim() to a geom_area plot sometimes *increases* the range
shown on the *y* axis. Can that be right? Example: The following
produces the area plot I would expect: The y scale on the chart ranges
from 0 to 3.:

some_data <- data.frame(x = c(1,2,3,4,5), y = c(2,3,2,3,2))
qplot(data = some_data, x = x, y = y, geom = "area")

But now, the following results in a y scale ranging from 0 to 5 (even
though, clearly, the maximum y can be no greater than in the previous
example):

last_plot() + xlim(c(1,3))

Indeed, last_plot() + xlim(c(2,3)) results in a y-axis that ranges
from 0 to 7! What am I missing here? (The same behaviour is observed
if I write out the plot in full, rather than using last_plot() and
also if I use scale_x_continuous() rather than xlim()). However, using
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2,3)) produces the plot I would expect --
with the y scale ranging from 0 to 3 as in the original plot.

I wouldn't mind, but it's extremely convenient to have an automatic y
scale in my actual application; unfortunately, the y scale chosen
automatically is so large that the graph is unreadably tiny; using
coord_cartesian() is a pain because I have an awful lot of points and
the chart takes forever to draw.

Any help (or enlightenment) greatly appreciated.

James

[R version 2.11.1 and ggplot 0.8.8 on OS X 10.6.4]

messages.subject: Stacked ggplot chart does not look accurate.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

These data compose the first bar of the graph. Naturally, the sum of
these four values of C2G equals the y value of the bar (about 14.198):
> cog[1:4,]
  Quarter        Segment        C2G
1 2008 Q1 Professional D  0.7509433
2 2008 Q1 Professional M  7.4151935
3 2008 Q1         Home D -0.4347982
4 2008 Q1         Home M  6.4669215

This is the code I'm using:
stackedchart <- ggplot(cog, aes(x=Quarter, y=C2G,
fill=factor(Segment)))
stackedchart <- stackedchart + layer(
geom="bar",
stat="identity",
position="stack")
stackedchart

I expect that the stacked "2008 Q1" bar have four factors each with a
unique color in this single bar. But the result only has three colors.
The smallest "Home D" value of -0.435 is missing.

Note that even though the bar only has three visible factors, the
stacked bar "begins" slightly below the x-axis at y = -0.435. This
tells me that the negative "Home D" value is included in the
calculations--it's just not visible.

Why does this happen?
Is there any way to make it look right?
Does the resulting warning message "Stacking not well defined when
ymin != 0" have anything to do with it and, if so, how do I make it
well defined?

I'm a new R user. Any help you all provide is much appreciated!

-Raphael

messages.body_plain:
hi

this is because the heights of the excluded data are stacked on the
unshown x value, that is, NA.

I dont know which way is better to fix, but putting below beforehand is easy:

pos_stack <- function(df, width) {
  if (nrow(df) == 1) return(df)

  n <- nrow(df) + 1
  y <- with(df, ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(y), 0, y))
  if(all(is.na <http://is.na>(df$x))){
    heights <- rep(0, n)
  }else{
    heights <- c(0, cumsum(y))
  }

  within(df, {
    ymin <- heights[-n]
    ymax <- heights[-1]
  })
}

assignInNamespace("pos_stack", pos_stack, pos="package:ggplot2")

messages.subject: Re: Efficent way of creating a contour
messages.subject_clean: Efficent way of creating a contour
messages.body_plain:
Couldn't you automate the production of the lines?  Use contourLines
to calculate the contours, then pick the appropriate level, and use
some basic geometry to work out where evenly spaced lines would
intersect with the curve.  It would probably take a couple of hours to
work out the details, but once you had it, it would save a lot of time
for future plots.

Hadley

On Tue, Oct 5, 2010 at 2:23 PM, Brian Weaver <the...@iastate.edu> wrote:
> All,
>
> I have been working on a constrained optimization problem where I find the
> solution graphically (think Lagrange multipliers).  The idea is I want to
> find the number of items (n) and the number of measurements per item (m)
> that minimizes some cost function subject to the constraint that the
> estimation precision of a function of interest (a standard error) is less
> than a certain value.  So the idea behind the plot is to have a contour that
> shows the contours of the cost function, the contours of the standard error,
> and a region that is not allowed since these values of (n,m) do not satisfy
> the constraint.  My professor wants me to "cross hatch out" the region that
> is not allowed.  Attached to this email is one of these plots so that you
> can better understand my description.  The dashed lines represent the
> contours for the standard error and the thick solid contours represent the
> cost function.  Also the asterisk is the optimum point.  I can do this plot
> by hand, but, one plot takes around 1-2 hours to create.  My question is is
> anyone familiar of a quicker way of doing this?  Currently the way I do it
> is create the contours and then add a geom_line for each individual line in
> the cross hatch region.  My code is below and I am attaching a data set that
> was used to create the plot.  I thank you all for your help ahead of time.
>
> Brian
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> dat <- read.table("your directory here...constrained_optim.txt",header = T)
>
> #Selecting the values that satisfy the constraint and saving as a separate
> object
> t.id <http://t.id> <- which(dat$SE <= 0.8)
> xx <- dat[t.id <http://t.id>,]
> tt <- which(xx[,3] == min(xx[,3]))
> xx[tt,]  ##Solution to optimum problem
>
> ##Creating the plot object
> v <- ggplot(dat,aes(x = n, y = m, z = cost))
> p <- v + geom_contour(breaks = seq(48600,80000,by = 7500),size = 1 ,color =
> "black" )+
> stat_contour(data = dat,aes(x = n,y = m, z = SE),
>              lty = 2, breaks = c(0.7906603,0.75,0.7)) +
> geom_point(aes(x = dat$n, y = dat$m), size =0) +
> geom_point(aes(x = xx[tt,1],y = xx[tt,2]),shape = 8,size = 4)+theme_bw() +
> ylab("Number of Measurements (m)") + xlab("Number of Units (n)")+
> geom_text(aes(x = 11.3, y = 20),label = 49,angle = 45, size = 4, hjust = 0)+

> geom_text(aes(x = 20, y = 8.8),label = 0.7, size =3, hjust = 0)
> p
>
> #Now adding the cross hatch region
> pp <- p+geom_line(aes(x = c(19,20),y = c(3,4)) )+

messages.body_plain:
Well, it's a negative value more than a negative height in my view.

Perhaps I shouldn't but I was expecting something similar to Excel. In
Excel, all four elements would be stacked. The negative "Home D" value
would begin at y=- 0.435 and extend to y = 0. The other three elements
would stack on top of that. In the end, the top of the graph would
have y = sum of all elements - Home D = 14.198 - 0.435. Effectively,
the length of the bar is the sum of the elements (14.198) but the max
y value is 14.198 - 0.435.

It seems to me like you're suggesting that negative values can't be
stacked in ggplot?

In fact... there are negative values in all Segment levels when I look
at the entire dataset (2008 Q1 - 2014 Q4) but "Home D" is the only
level that "disappears". It's almost as if whenever "Home D" is
negative, ggplot uses it's negative value as the starting y-value for
the other three stacked values??? That's what it seems like, at
least.

By the way, I find your Elegant Graphics book very helpful. I received
it from Amazon yesterday.

Thanks,

Raphael

Hi Raphael,

On Wed, Oct 6, 2010 at 11:09 PM, Raphael <rhv....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Well, it's a negative value more than a negative height in my view.
>
> Perhaps I shouldn't but I was expecting something similar to Excel. In
> Excel, all four elements would be stacked. The negative "Home D" value
> would begin at y=- 0.435 and extend to y = 0. The other three elements
> would stack on top of that. In the end, the top of the graph would
> have y = sum of all elements - Home D = 14.198 - 0.435. Effectively,
> the length of the bar is the sum of the elements (14.198) but the max
> y value is 14.198 - 0.435.
>
> It seems to me like you're suggesting that negative values can't be
> stacked in ggplot?

This can be done quite easily actually. You just need to plot the
positive and negative values in separate layers, like this:

cog$pn <- factor(sign(cog$C2G), labels=c("-", "+"))

stackedchart <- ggplot(cog, aes(x=Quarter, y=C2G,
fill=factor(Segment)))
stackedchart <- stackedchart + layer(
geom="bar",
stat="identity",

position="stack",
data=subset(cog, pn == "+"))

stackedchart <- stackedchart + layer(
geom="bar",
stat="identity",

position="stack",
data=subset(cog, pn == "-"))
stackedchart + geom_hline(yintercept=0)

>
> In fact... there are negative values in all Segment levels when I look
> at the entire dataset (2008 Q1 - 2014 Q4) but "Home D" is the only
> level that "disappears". It's almost as if whenever "Home D" is
> negative, ggplot uses it's negative value as the starting y-value for
> the other three stacked values??? That's what it seems like, at
> least.

It's there, underneath the others. Try

stackedchart <- ggplot(cog, aes(x=Quarter, y=C2G,
fill=factor(Segment)))
stackedchart <- stackedchart + layer(
geom="bar",
stat="identity",

position="stack",
alpha=.5)
stackedchart

and you will see it.

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Transparent Boxes Overlayed on Plots
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

Is there any way of placing a transparent "box" over a region in
ggplot2? Suppose you had a time series plotted on the horizontal axis
and that time series could be categorized. So in R you would have the
time series as one variable and then the grouping variable as another.
What I am wondering is if you can overlay a transparent box over the
time series plot based on the grouping variable?

So in the example below I would like the plot (both facets) to have a
transparent box over the 1-4 region of "x" and then another
transparent box (either of a different colour or different shade of
grey) over the 5-8 region of "x". The variable "label" could be used
potential to distinguish the different regions.

library(ggplot2)
x <-runif(80, 1,8)
data <- as.data.frame(x)
data$y <--runif(80, 0, 125)
data$z <- factor(c("A","A","B","B"))
data$label<- with(data, ifelse(x<4,"Left", "Right"))

pg <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~z, ncol=1,scales="free_y") +
  theme_bw()
pg

I hope I have explained the problem clear enough.

Thanks in advance!

Sam

messages.body_plain:
On Oct 7, 2:19 pm, Sam <tonightstheni...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello there,
>
> Is there any way of placing a transparent "box" over a region in
> ggplot2? Suppose you had a time series plotted on the horizontal axis
> and that time series could be categorized. So in R you would have the
> time series as one variable and then the grouping variable as another.
> What I am wondering is if you can overlay a transparent box over the
> time series plot based on the grouping variable?
>
> So in the example below I would like the plot (both facets) to have a
> transparent box over the 1-4 region of "x" and then another
> transparent box (either of a different colour or different shade of
> grey) over the 5-8 region of "x". The variable "label" could be used
> potential to distinguish the different regions.
>
> library(ggplot2)
> x <-runif(80, 1,8)
> data <- as.data.frame(x)
> data$y <--runif(80, 0, 125)
> data$z <- factor(c("A","A","B","B"))
> data$label<- with(data, ifelse(x<4,"Left", "Right"))
>
> pg <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +
>   geom_point(colour = 2) +
>   facet_wrap(~z, ncol=1,scales="free_y") +
>   theme_bw()
> pg

Thanks for the example.  You can put an annotation of this sort on
fairly easily, but it is actually easiest to do if you make a
secondary annotation data set (either "by hand" or derived from your
original data set in some way):

data_annot <- data.frame(left=c(1,5), right=c(4,8),
label=c("Left","Right"))

ggplot(data) +
  geom_rect(data=data_annot, aes(xmin=left, xmax=right, fill=label,
    ymin=-Inf, ymax=Inf), alpha=0.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x,y), colour=2) +
  facet_wrap(~z, ncol=1, scales="free_y") +
  theme_bw()

A couple of things of note.  The aes() call in ggplot() has been
moved.  That is because if it is there, every layer looks for both "x"
and "y", and the data set for the annotation layer does not have it
and so you get an error.  The aes() is now in the geom_point() call.
Also, I put the geom_rect() layer before the geom_point() layer so
that it is drawn below it.  To make it somewhat transparent, I made
the alpha 0.2.  The y limits are set to -Inf and Inf so that the bars
cover the whole vertical range, no matter what it is (the scales don't
expand to try and take -Inf and Inf in).  Fill colors can be set with
one of the scale_fill()'s

You can even go a step further and put the specific filling colors in
the annotation set:

data_annot <- data.frame(left=c(1,5), right=c(4,8),
fill=c("gray80","gray90"))

ggplot(data) +
  geom_rect(data=data_annot, aes(xmin=left, xmax=right, fill=fill,
    ymin=-Inf, ymax=Inf)) +
  geom_point(aes(x,y), colour=2) +
  facet_wrap(~z, ncol=1, scales="free_y") +
  scale_fill_identity(legend=FALSE) +
  theme_bw()

Here I used scale_fill_identity() to indicate that the value of the
variable actually has the color names to be used.  Also, I got rid of
the transparency; since it is behind the points, you may not need it
(although if not transparent, the grid lines can't be seen).  If you
really want to use transparency, set the fill to black and use alpha
as an aesthetic set to an appropriate variable in the annotation data
set:

data_annot <- data.frame(left=c(1,5), right=c(4,8), alpha=c(0.2, 0.1))

ggplot(data) +
  geom_rect(data=data_annot, aes(xmin=left, xmax=right, alpha=alpha),
    ymin=-Inf, ymax=Inf, fill="black") +
  geom_point(aes(x,y), colour=2) +
  facet_wrap(~z, ncol=1, scales="free_y") +
  scale_alpha_identity(legend=FALSE) +
  theme_bw()

Where you have to get scale_alpha_identity() from
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/f8576a044fd09944
(code from Hadley reproduced below):

scale_alpha_identity <- function (name = NULL, breaks = NULL, labels =
NULL, formatter = NULL,
    legend = TRUE, ...)  ScaleIdentity$new(name = name, breaks =
breaks, labels = labels,
    formatter = formatter, legend = legend, variable = "alpha", ...)

> I hope I have explained the problem clear enough.
>
> Thanks in advance!
>
> Sam

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.body_plain:
Sarah,

It's pretty hard to say without your data what is going on. Generally, shape should be a factor of some sort, which would indicate to me that you shouldn't easily be able to simply switch Group and Gap with scale_x_continuous() since they are likely to be discrete. Have you tried increasing the width of the bar? 0.06 is kind of small and if your scale differs between the two then maybe 0.06 is so small that you can't see it. Set it to 1 or 10 and just see what happens.

As far as putting points next to each other you could try setting position="jitter" in geom_point() or or use geom_jitter(). I'm not sure if you can connect points with a line if you use jitter though.

I assume that limits is something like this:
limits<- aes(ymax=mean+se, ymin=mean-se)

ggplot(data = group.means.lat.gap, aes(x = Gap, y = MeanLatency))+
geom_point(aes(shape=Group), size=3)+
geom_errorbar(limits, width=0.06)+
geom_line(size=1)+
scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(-200,0))+

messages.body_plain:
This is the 'ol double plot problem.  You are plotting a box plot and
a point plot (geom_jitter).  The outlier point is plotted by
geom_boxplot and by geom_jitter.  You can see this more clearly if you
set a color for geom_jitter().

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

There are a few problems here, and in the process I believe you've exposed a potential 'gotcha' in ggplot2.

2010/10/9 Manuel Spínola <mspin...@gmail.com>

> Dear list members,
>
> I have 2 questions (data set and plot attached attached):
>
> This is my code:
>
> p = ggplot(alt, aes(arrecife, altura))
>
> p +  stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "bar")
>
> + stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_normal", colour = "red", geom = "errorbar", width=0.25)
>
> + scale_y_continuous(name ="Altura (cm)") + xlab("Arrecife") + aes(fill=arrecife)
>
> + scale_fill_grey()
>
> + scale_x_discrete(labels=c("Borde Coralino Blue Hole", "Arrecife Posterior HMC AR", "Arrecife Frontal HMC AR", "Parches de Arrecife HMC AR", "Arrecife Posterior HMC AC"), breaks=levels(alt$arrecife))
>
> + opts(legend.position = "none") + opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle=30, hjust=1))
>

Firstly, this is (sigh) *another* dynamite plot, so I find it necessary to point you to

http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/twiki/pub/Main/TatsukiRcode/Poster3.pdf

To add to the poster's contents, you are using each bar to represent an average, which could be done with far less ink by replacing it with a point, either in a different color or an enlarged size (or both). Less ink, no loss of information, no domination of the plot by needless, distracting bars.

> 1. When using stat_summary the y axis limits is too wide (from 0 to 200) I think because the raw data but I need something from 0 to 30.  If I set the limits with coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 30)) what I am doing is zooming and the y axis scale doesn't show up very well, loosing the numbers in the axis.

I'm wondering what goes on with mean_cl_normal, as I'll explain below...

>
> 2.  The axis label text show blurry when I set up an angle for the text.

Why can't you flip the axis so that the labels can be seen without having to risk whiplash? Example below.

>
> Any suggestion how to fix these 2 problems?
> Thank you very much in advance.
>

After reading in your data, I decided to do groupwise summaries using ddply() in the plyr package, returning the group mean and standard error, and then computing the lower and upper 95% large sample confidence limits (Wald interval). The result is in the object altSumm.

se <- function(x) sd(x)/sqrt(length(x))
altSumm <- ddply(alt, 'arrecife', summarise, mean = mean(altura), se = se(altura))
altSumm <- transform(altSumm, ll = mean - 1.96 * se, ul = mean + 1.96 * se)

p2p below is a simplified version of your plot, sans labels. When I combine it with error bar plots computed from altSumm, there are noticeable differences in the confidence limit widths, but even worse, offset means! I could understand somewhat different SEs, but different means altogether doesn't make sense. The black dots are the group means from your original plot that replaced the bars. With altSumm, I have the opportunity to double check the calculations, and did check them against other functions such as tapply() and aggregate(), getting the same answers. This makes me wonder what's going on with 'mean_cl_normal' in stat_summary()...this hypothesis is investigated below.

In addition, the mean_cl_normal results suggest that one group is significantly higher than the others, but a one-way ANOVA failed to confirm that (p = 0.428). The CIs produced from altSumm appear to be more consistent with the ANOVA results (not shown, but simple to do with aov() ).  This is the code to produce the attached plot:

p2 <- ggplot(alt, aes(arrecife, altura))
p2p <- p2 + stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) + ylim(0, 30) +

          stat_summary(fun.data = "mean_cl_normal", colour = "red", geom = "errorbar", width=0.25)

p2p + geom_errorbar(data = altSumm, aes(arrecife, mean, ymin = mean - se,
                                        ymax = mean + se), colour = 'blue', width = 0.25)

The graph below is a combination stripchart/error bar plot, where the error bar designates the endpoints of a group's approximate 95% CI for mean altura. Alpha transparency is used to lighten the points, a line connecting the means is added and the plot is flipped so that one can read the group labels easily. This plot shows a couple of things: (i) your data are not normally distributed within group, which makes me wonder about the validity of the confidence intervals for mean altura; (ii) the data contain several distinct outliers - since the mean is known to be sensitive to the presence of outliers, a more resistant estimator of center may be called for, such as the median, from which you could obtain a reasonable interval estimate by bootstrapping.
A more appropriate thing to have done here would have been to compare group distributions with a combination of boxplots and stripcharts, which you could use to justify a measure of center other than the mean. (Groupwise density plots would also be useful.) Transformation is an option, but back transformation of endpoints is always an issue of interpretation...

ggplot(alt, aes(arrecife, altura)) +
   geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), alpha = 0.3) +
   geom_errorbar(data = altSumm, aes(arrecife, mean, ymin = mean - 1.96 * se,
          ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), colour = 'red', width = 0.25, size = 1) +
   geom_line(data = altSumm, aes(arrecife, mean, group = 1), colour = 'blue') +
   xlab("Arrecife") + ylab("Altura (cm)") +

   scale_x_discrete(labels=c("Borde Coralino Blue Hole", "Arrecife Posterior HMC AR",
                            "Arrecife Frontal HMC AR", "Parches de Arrecife HMC AR",
                            "Arrecife Posterior HMC AC"), breaks=levels(alt$arrecife)) +

   coord_flip()

The plot below is a variation on the error bar plot over the range (0, 30) on the response scale, where the axis are flipped to improve readability of the arrecife labels.

q <- ggplot(altSumm, aes(x = arrecife, y = mean, ymin = ll, ymax = ul))
q + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_errorbar(colour = 'red', width = 0.25) +
    geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = 'blue') + ylim(0, 30) +
    xlab("") + ylab('Mean Altura') +

    scale_x_discrete(labels=c("Borde Coralino Blue Hole", "Arrecife Posterior HMC AR",
                            "Arrecife Frontal HMC AR", "Parches de Arrecife HMC AR",
                            "Arrecife Posterior HMC AC"), breaks=levels(alt$arrecife)) +

    coord_flip()

The warning message below indicates that before stat_summary() does the calculations of mean and standard error for input into mean_cl_normal, it removes all the altura values larger than 30. This would explain the reduced means and shorter confidence limits in the attached plot using your ggplot() code.
Warning messages:
1: Removed 106 rows containing missing values (stat_summary).
2: Removed 106 rows containing missing values (stat_summary).

Hadley quite reasonably recommends doing as much of the work outside of ggplot2 as possible. By using an external data frame of summary data as a double check, I believe we have identified a potential 'gotcha' when using stat_summary() in a ggplot() and plotting over a restricted range. This doesn't appear to be a sum of layer 'main effects', but rather an interaction.

Checking the means and standard errors under this hypothesis,

# altura <= 30:
> with(subset(alt, altura <= 30), tapply(altura, arrecife, mean))
       a        b        c        d        e
17.79832 12.25385 11.83607 11.74803 10.71739
> with(subset(alt, altura <= 30), tapply(altura, arrecife, se))
        a         b         c         d         e
0.6588371 0.5801642 0.7188748 0.7348834 0.9558682

# all data:
> with(alt, tapply(altura, arrecife, mean))
       a        b        c        d        e
22.46667 18.82000 19.91333 20.21333 16.10000
> with(alt, tapply(altura, arrecife, se))
        a         b         c         d         e
0.9491155 1.9017729 1.8018866 2.1657407 3.9614726

That appears to explain the differences in the attached plot...

Let me end with a provocative question...would this problem have been easier to detect with bars to represent the means?

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am plotting a PCA plot with size and colour determined by the same
variable, with the size value reversed:
> ggplot(pcaCombo,aes(x=PC1,y=PC2)) + geom_point(aes(color=all_probeset_percent_called,size=all_probeset_percent_called)) + scale_size(trans="reverse")

This produces two keys.  If I remove the scale_size command I only get
one key.  Is there a way to combine the colour and size key when the
size scale has beed reversed?

Thanks

Dan

messages.subject: Re: Re: Using ggplot2 to plot predicted probabilities
messages.subject_clean: Using ggplot2 to plot predicted probabilities
messages.body_plain:
You might want to look at Prof Harrell's rms package which is a remarkable collection of regression tools reflecting his philosophy, including many graphical displays.

It now (as of V3.0?) produces data frames from the Predict command and these df slide nicely into ggplot2.

Harrell and Hadley are clearly friends and while Harrell's current rms package does not yet make (extensive use) of ggplot, I suspect that plans are afoot.

I will say that have had less success (probably reflecting lack of effort) in converting Harrell's elegant bplot (heat-map) outputs into something equally elegant in ggplot2. But the fautl lies not in the software, but in the operator.  For displaying categorical predictors, etc, you can start with the rms standard outputs and then use the dataframes which get generated by Predict to feed ggplot. That said, rms has a very particular and specific take on things like bootstrapping, calibration, and to use it well really requires engaging with Harrell's larger methodological and statistical perspective.

---------------------------
Robert C James, PhD

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The problem is that with five factors each at two levels, there are 32 factor combinations. I suppose you could combine the levels of two factors twice to produce a 4 x 4 plot, and then make one plot with all 16 combinations at level 0 of the fifth factor and another at level 1 of the fifth factor. You could then use the 'paste two graphs on one page' trick using the ideas from section 8.4 of Hadley's book. I suspect that plot will be a bit cramped, but it's one approach to the problem...

HTH,
Dennis

Now, I found that having several categorical predictors, and even some of them with several levels, is challenging for showing the results, and even more challenging to make the plots.  I tried the effects package from John Fox, but the plot for categorical predictor is not what I would like for this type of variables.

> >

But the fautl lies not in the software, but in the operator.  For displaying categorical predictors, etc, you can start with the rms standard outputs and then use the dataframes which get generated by Predict to feed ggplot. That said, rms has a very particular and specific take on things like bootstrapping, calibration, and to use it well really requires engaging with Harrell's larger methodological and statistical perspective.

messages.body_plain:
I haven't taken a close look at your data, but the discussion makes me think of fuzzy set analysis.  Might be relevant if you can convert your factor levels into set memberships (your dependent is already binary, right?)  It gives results in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions which can really help interpretation of different routes to your outcome.  Of course if no one knows it in your literature then it's a hard sell.  This paper is a good intro:

Fiss PC (2007) A Set-theoretic Approach to Organizational Configurations. Academy of Management Review. 32:1180-1198.

--J

messages.subject: Re: confidence intervals with geom_smooth()
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 12, 12:52 pm, Shai <shain...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi!
>
> Maybe this is for beginners but I still cant get that right... How do
> I use the geom_smooth to draw the dashed 95% confidence intervals
> above and below my trend line? I got to the point where I make the
> gray fill disappear, now I only have to add the two dashed borders!
>
> xvalues <- 0:10
> yvalues <- c(1,3,2,4,5.5,6,2,9,7,8.2,9)
> d <- data.frame(xvalues,yvalues)
> p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=xvalues,y=yvalues))
> p+geom_point()+geom_smooth(method="lm",fill="NA")

geom_smooth does not have a line around it, so there isn't any way to
make it show up.  geom_ribbon, on the other hand, does.

p+geom_point()+geom_smooth(method="lm",fill="NA")+
stat_smooth(method="lm",fill=NA,colour="black",linetype=2,geom="ribbon")

You can adjust the color and linetype as you like.

> The borders ARE the confidence intervals right?
>
> Thanks,
> Shai

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: confidence intervals with geom_smooth()
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

If you don't like the contiguity of the confidence envelopes at the extremes of the x's, here's the brute force approach: compute the linear model, get the upper and lower limits from lm, concatenate to the original data, and use it as input into ggplot():

xvalues <- 0:10
yvalues <- c(1,3,2,4,5.5,6,2,9,7,8.2,9)
d <- data.frame(xvalues,yvalues)

# fit model and get lower/upper 95% confidence limits at the observed x's
m <- lm(yvalues ~ xvalues, data = d)
mp <- predict(m, interval = 'conf')

# bind predictions to original data and plot
d2 <- cbind(d, mp)
p <- ggplot(d2, aes(x = xvalues, y = yvalues))
p + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE) +
    geom_line(aes(y = upr), color = 'red', linetype = 2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = lwr), color = 'red', linetype = 2)

A few extra lines of code, but nothing difficult.

HTH,
Dennis

I have done some more work on your graph.  Dennis's suggestion can in
fact be simplified a little bit.  The following code combines two sets
of factors to display four variables in facets, and uses the fifth as
a categorical variable in the plot itself.

It helps, of course, to understand that the data really is one
variable, with upper and lower confidence limits.

lcie <- paste("cielo.raso", 0:1)
lpis <- paste("piso", 0:1)
lpar <- paste("paredes", 0:1)

d$iluminacion <- as.factor(lilu[d$iluminacion + 1])
d$animales    <- as.factor(lani[d$animales + 1])

messages.body_plain:
I think Hadley may have misunderstood (or I'm misunderstanding).

   Suppose you have (or can construct) a design matrix X; the
coefficients of
the linear predictor p; and the variance-covariance matrix of the
coefficients V.

  Then the predicted values of the linear predictor are LP = X %*% p
             "         "            "       "        response
plogis(LP) [i.e., inverse-link transform of LP]

  The variance of the linear predictor predictions is V_LP =  X %*% V
%*% t(X) [I think; play around with
this until it makes sense]
   If you want the confidence intervals of the response, you should use

  plogis(LP +/- 1.96 * sqrt(V_LP))

  if you construct an appropriate data frame with pred, pred_lo,
pred_hi, you can then use geom_line()
to add the prediction and geom_ribbon() [or geom_linerange()] to add the
confidence intervals on the prediction.

   Ben Bolker

On Oct 14, 4:10 pm, Brandon Hurr <bhiv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> It's pretty ugly, but...
>
> dplot + geom_bar(width=1)

Thank you! I knew I'd seem such an option before, but couldn't find it
in ?geom_bar 8-)

Even with the "width" argument, I needed to debug a bit before it
worked. I describe my case here for posterity:

My actual data frame was a molten crosstabulation, like this:

> df <- read.table(header=TRUE, textConnection("
Species variable value
  Apple      Fat   0.1
 Orange      Fat   0.2
  Apple  Protein   0.2
 Orange  Protein   0.4
  Apple    Carbo   0.7
 Orange    Carbo   0.4
"))

The final solution was this:

> ggplot(df) + geom_bar(aes(x=Species, y=value, fill=variable), width=1)

This line below is what I started with. I didn't realize that
stat="identity" is superfluous when both x and y are given. Also,
stacking seems to be the default.

> ggplot(df) + geom_bar(aes(x=Species, y=value, fill=variable), stat="identity", position="stack")

Adding "width" to the latter command has no effect; the argument is
just ignored.

> ggplot(df) + geom_bar(aes(x=Species, y=value, fill=variable), stat="identity", position="stack", width=1)

I guess the reason I don't need stat_identity is that I have only one
row per "Species" and "variable". The default aggregation seems to be
averaging (ggplot(rbind(df, df)) + ... looks identical to ggplot(df)
+ ...), so that the data pass through unchanged.

Thank you very much for your help!

Regards,
Jon Olav

This graph doesn't make sense because I have chosen silly ranges for
the predictors, but the general idea should be OK.

coefs <- c(-4.95,0.003,0.755)

vc <- matrix(c(1.16,-0.00028,-0.28,
               -0.00028,-0.0000011,-0.00011,
               -0.28,-0.00011,0.102),
             nrow=3,byrow=TRUE)

library(ggplot2)

## since we have two continuous predictors and want to show
## uncertainty, we're pretty much stuck with a conditioning plot
## i.e., 'slicing' one predictor into discrete categories;
## very hard to construct perspective/contour plots that are actually
## interpretable when we are superimposing either data or confidence
## intervals on the surface

predframe <- expand.grid(x=1:100,y=seq(0,88,length=9))
mm <- cbind(1,as.matrix(predframe)) ## model matrix
pred_eta <- mm %*% coefs
se_pred_eta <- diag(mm %*% tcrossprod(vc,mm))

pred <- plogis(pred_eta)
pred_lo <- plogis(pred_eta-1.96*se_pred_eta)
pred_hi <- plogis(pred_eta+1.96*se_pred_eta)

predframe <- cbind(predframe,yfac=factor(predframe$y),
                   pred,pred_lo,pred_hi)

ggplot(predframe,aes(x=x,y=pred,ymin=pred_lo,ymax=pred_hi))+
  geom_line()+geom_ribbon(alpha=0.5,colour=NA)+
  facet_wrap(~yfac)

pl + opts (axis.text.y = theme_text(size=20, hjust=1,
colour=alpha("black", c(.3, 1, 1))))

pl + opts (axis.text.y = theme_text(size=20, hjust=1,
colour=alpha("black", daply(d.frame, .(city), function(x)

Hi All,

I would like a graph that has two sets of data plotted together. I've
been using the 'melt' command for this and it's working fine. I'm
encountering a problem is when I try to put error bars on the data
points. When I melt my data frame the error values are included in the
same column as the data. So far I haven't been able to find any way to
create two value columns using 'melt', is there an alternative?

I've also tried calling two separate data frames which seems to
confuse R, I get an error message instead of a plot

For reference -

DF <- read.table("LightCurve.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",")
new.data<-melt(DF,id.var="X",na.rm=FALSE)

####For error bars - this is for when I try to use separate data
frames
error <- read.table("LCrror2.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",")
new.error<-melt(error,id.var="Val",na.rm=FALSE)

G <- ggplot(new.data,aes(x=X,y=-value))+
geom_point(shape = variable) +
scale_x_continuous("JD - 2450000") +
scale_y_continuous("Magnitude Difference",breaks = c(-13, -12.5, -12,
-11.5, -11), label = c("13", "12.5", "12", "11.5", "11")) +
coord_cartesian()

G + labs(shape = "Filter")

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Fri, Oct 15, 2010 at 8:04 AM, JohnStJohn <johnthes...@gmail.com> wrote:
> So I have two two column tables avg_10 and avg_15. The first column is
> a number and the second column is the frequency of that number in my
> data.
>
> I made a nice pseudo density plot that shows the distribution of
> avg_10 and avg_15 overlaid. I added fill to it by setting aes( fill =
> "10mer") and  in the second layer aes(fill="15mer" ), then it just
> treats each layer as a separate color which is nice. There are some
> issues though. When I do it that way the legend title is stuck at
> "10mer", and my x and y axes aren't changing when I try to set xlab
> and ylab. How can I either 1. change the legend, x and y axis label,
> or 2. do this same plot differently so I have better controle over the
> axis and legend titles. Thanks for your time!

Here's one approach (caveat emptor: idle speculation since I have no ability to test it on your data):

* combine the two data frames into one, using the names '10Mer' and '15Mer' as factor labels to distinguish the two - these will be the default labels in the legend, with default legend title Kmer. Change as appropriate if you want something else.

avg <- rbind(avg_10, avg_15)
avg$Kmer <- factor(rep(c('10Mer', '15Mer'), c(nrow(avg_10), nrow(avg_15)) ))

# plot
m <- ggplot(avg, aes(x = V1, fill = Kmer))
m  + geom_density(aes(weight = V2), alpha = 0.8) +
        xlab('Average Kmer Frequency') + ylab('Number of Reads') + scale_x_log10()

HTH,
Dennis

Alexa

Melt will do what you need.  However, there is a small semantic error
in your code.  The parameter for melt() is id.vars="x".  Notice that
you used id.var="x", i.e. there is an "s" missing in your code.
Because of this, melt() will use the default behaviour, which isn't
what you are looking for.  I suspect if you fix this one line of code,
your original approach will work.

Andrie

Hello.

The code below shows my intentions. I would like to have error bars
for each of the stacked bars, but in the plot that I have managed to
produce the "position" of the centre of the error bars is not the
location of the top of each stacked bar.

Pedro.

library(ggplot2)

stack_code <- factor(rep(c('A','B'),4))
treatment <- factor(rep(c('a','a','b','b'),2))
facet_code <- factor(c(rep(1,4),rep(2,4)))
resp <- c(10,1,12,3,9,2,11,3)
SEM <- rep(0.3,8)
test.data <- data.frame(treatment,stack_code,facet_code,resp,SEM)

p <- ggplot(test.data, aes(fill=stack_code, y=resp, x=treatment))
p1 <- p  + geom_bar(stat="identity") + facet_wrap(~facet_code)
p2 <- p1 + geom_errorbar(aes(ymax = resp + SEM, ymin=resp - SEM),
width=0.1)
print(p2)

messages.subject: Re: Stacked bars with error_bar: how?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Let me first point you here:
http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/wiki/Main/DynamitePlots

Please read the one-page poster linked near the bottom of the page (Poster3.pdf) and the last paragraph at the bottom of the page. This will explain the transformation of your plot I am about to suggest below.

I created a new factor for names of the facets, which should be a little more informative than '1, 2'.

To replace the unnecessary, distracting and visually overpowering bars, we plot points for the (mean) response instead. These points have precisely the same amount of information as the bars, with much less ink expended.

stack_code <- factor(rep(c('A','B'),4))
treatment <- factor(rep(c('a','a','b','b'),2))
facet_code <- factor(c(rep(1,4),rep(2,4)))
resp <- c(10,1,12,3,9,2,11,3)
SEM <- rep(0.3,8)
test.data <- data.frame(treatment, stack_code, facet_code, resp, SEM)

test.data$facet <- factor(rep(c('Facet 1', 'Facet 2'), each = 4))

p <- ggplot(test.data, aes(x = treatment, y = resp, colour = stack_code))
p + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymax = resp + SEM, ymin = resp - SEM), width = 0.1, size = 1) +
      facet_wrap(~ facet) +
      scale_colour_manual('Stack code', values = c('A' = 'red', 'B' = 'blue')) +
      xlab('Treatment') + ylab('Response')

The size parameters in geom_point() and geom_errorbar() are chosen to make them stand out a little bit more - the use of more dramatic colors has the same purpose.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: problem with ylab under Mac Snow Leopard
messages.subject_clean: problem with ylab under Mac Snow Leopard
messages.body_plain:
# developed a multi-colored ribbon plot to illustrate call center performance
# working under Mac Snow Leopard OS X 10.6.4
# and R 2.11.1 GUI 1.34 Leopard build 32-bit (5589)
# everything is working fine except for labels on the vertical axis
# why does xlab work but not ylab?
# here is the code....

library(ggplot2)

x.hour <- seq(from=0,to=23)
ymax.bottomwhite <- ymin.percentile <- c(8.0,8.5,6.0,10.0,11.0,15.0,8.5,8.0,12.0,11.0,11.0,10.0,10.0,10.0,16.0,14.0,11.0,11.0,11.0,11.5,8.0,6.0,8.0,5.5)
ymin.topwhite <- ymax.percentile <- c(15.03333,15.23333,10.33333,13.00000,12.00000,18.00000,19.01667,12.96667,21.00000,20.00000,20.91667,20.20000,19.85000,15.91667,24.86667,21.01667,19.95000,24.96667,17.75000,18.10000,15.50000,11.00000,11.20000,8.00000)

ymin.bottomwhite <- greenmin <- rep(0,length=24)
greenmax <- rep(15,length=24)

yellowmin <- rep(15,length=24)
yellowmax <- rep(20,length=24)

redmin <- rep(20,length=24)
ymax.topwhite <- redmax <- rep(30,length=24)

words.for.plot.title <- "Call Center Wait-Time Report \n(Displayed Range is 50th to 85th Percentiles)"

ggobject <- ggplot() + geom_ribbon(data=demand.calls.data.frame, mapping=aes(x=x.hour, ymin=greenmin, ymax=greenmax), stat="identity",colour="white",fill="darkgreen")  + geom_ribbon(data=demand.calls.data.frame, mapping=aes(x=x.hour, ymin=yellowmin, ymax=yellowmax), stat="identity",colour="white",fill="yellow")  + geom_ribbon(data=demand.calls.data.frame, mapping=aes(x=x.hour, ymin=redmin, ymax=redmax), stat="identity",colour="white",fill="red")   + geom_ribbon(data=demand.calls.data.frame, mapping=aes(x=x.hour, ymin=ymin.topwhite, ymax=ymax.topwhite), stat="identity",colour="white",fill="white")      + geom_ribbon(data=demand.calls.data.frame, mapping=aes(x=x.hour, ymin=ymin.bottomwhite, ymax=ymax.bottomwhite), stat="identity",colour="white",fill="white")  + xlab("Hour of Day (24-Hour Clock)")  + ylab("Call Center Wait-Time (Seconds)") + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=15)) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=20)) + opts(title = words.for.plot.title) + theme_bw(base_size = 12) + scale_y_continuous("", limits = c(0, 30))

print(ggobject)

messages.subject: Re: Adding text to a plot (geom_pointrange)
messages.body_plain:
Manuel:
If you just want to add text, 'annotate' is probably the way to go:

dfa = data.frame(a = factor(c("18-25 años", "26-35 años", "36-45 años", "46-60 años", ">60 años"), levels=c("18-25 años", "26-35 años", "36-45 años", "46-60 años", ">60 años")), b = c(16, 42, 17, 20, 4))
limitesa <- aes(ymax =c(25, 53, 26, 29, 10) , ymin=c(0.9, 32, 10, 12, 1))

a = ggplot(dfa, aes(y=b, x=a)) + geom_pointrange(limitesa, size = 1) + xlab("Categoría de Edad") + ylab("Porcentaje (%)") + opts(legend.position = "none") + theme_bw()

a
a
a + annotate("text",x=0,y=55,label="a")

US Fish & Wildlife Service
California, USA

library("ggplot2")
library("reshape")

645.","AKO.645."))

error2 <- error$value

G <- ggplot(new.data,aes(x=X,y=-value))+
geom_point(aes(shape = variable)) +
scale_x_continuous("JD - 2450000") +
scale_y_continuous("Magnitude Difference",breaks = c(-13, -12.5, -12,
-11.5, -11), label = c("13", "12.5", "12", "11.5", "11")) +
coord_cartesian()

Graph <- G + labs(shape = "Filter")

Graph + geom_errorbar(aes(ymax = -value - error2, ymin = - value +
error2))

Thank you for your help! I appreciate it.

messages.body_plain:
I've run across a curious problem with stat_smooth(). I've found that
the manner in which the function fits a curve to the data points is
somehow dependent upon the limits placed upon the Y axis (changes to
the X axis have no effect). I have three sets of code below, and the
only difference is in ylim(). However, instead of just "zooming in/
out," the fit lines and the standard error shadings change quite
dramatically. It seems that the way they are drawn is dependent upon
the data points that are visible, rather than the full data set fed
into ggplot(data=). My first hope was that fullrange=T would fix it,
but no. I haven't been able to find any parameters that make the issue
go away or attenuate. Could you offer other avenues that I might
explore to solve this riddle?

Jim

Instead of using limits, using coord_cartesian() to "zoom" in.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel

On Mon, Oct 18, 2010 at 7:16 PM, Manuel Spínola <mspin...@gmail.com> wrote:

Great, thanks for the example.

>
> p = ggplot(geo1, aes(x, y))
> p + geom_point(aes(size = md)) + scale_size(name = "Indice", breaks = c(0.1,
> 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50)) + theme_bw()
>
> In the code I am setting the point size according to the variable md, but I
> also want the points to be in different colors (colour = md).

you just need to tell ggplot what you're telling me (literally!).

p + geom_point(aes(size = md, colour=md)) + scale_size(name =

"Indice", breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50)) + theme_bw()

>

> Regarding to the other question, the data set has 2 different groups
> (geographically different) and I would like to do 2 facets to show each
> group but with different limits for the x axis.  I am attaching a plot.

So you need a faceting variable.

p + geom_point(aes(size = md, color=md)) + scale_size(name = "Indice",
breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50)) + theme_bw() +
facet_grid(.~sitio, scales="free")

These are pretty standard features, have you browsed http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/?

messages.subject: Re: geom_point size and colour and different axis limits with facet
messages.subject_clean: geom_point size and colour and different axis limits with facet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

Are you trying to coordinate the colors and sizes in the same legend? If so, then you need to give both scales the same name and the same set of breaks (Hadley mentioned this the other day in another post.)  Does this work?

p <- ggplot(geo1, aes(x = x, y = y, size = md, colour = md))
p + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ sitio, scales = 'free') +
#    theme_bw() +

    scale_size(name = 'Indice',
                         breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50)) +

    scale_colour_gradientn(name = 'Indice', colours = topo.colors(9),

                         breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50)) +

    opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 8, vjust = 1)) +
    opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 8, hjust = 1))

Uncomment the line with theme_bw() if you want a white background instead.

HTH,
Dennis

Thanks for your help!

Aditya

Hi:

Sorry I didn't see the graph/data at the end of your message. I think this is what you want:

ggplot(resTmp) + geom_bar(aes(x = reorder(methodTransfo, me, mean), y = me)) +
     scale_fill_grey(start=0.8, end=0.1) +
     theme_bw(base_size=16) +
      xlab('methodTransfo')

The reorder() function is useful when you want to order the levels of a factor by some characteristic of another variable - in this case, the value of me.  Since there's only one value for me, any of min, max, mean, median would have worked.

HTH,
Dennis

Hi Adita,

I do not understand very well what you want (e.g. the order is as expected, maybe you want the inverse direction?), but let me try;

library(ggplot2)

load("resTmp.dat")

str(resTmp)

   b <- ggplot(resTmp)

   b <- b + geom_bar( aes(x=methodTransfo, y=me) ) + coord_flip()

   b <- b + scale_fill_grey(start=0.8, end=0.1)

   b <- b + theme_bw(base_size=16)

   print(b)

n <- length(levels(resTmp$methodTransfo))

resTmp$methodTransfo <- factor( resTmp$methodTransfo, levels = levels(resTmp$methodTransfo)[n:1] )

b %+% resTmp

messages.subject: Re: simple colour question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

You can use scale_colour_manual() to manually set the colour for each
level of your factor.
Here's the link to Hadley's website on it:
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_manual.html
There are also colour scales for gradients and the like which you may
find helpful.  Anyway, here is a little example where I change the
colours to blue and red and set the alpha to 1/5.

###################################
# load library
library(ggplot2)

# create some sample data
dat <- data.frame(A = 1:12, B = rep(1:2, each = 6), C = (1:12)^2)

# create base ggplot object
ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = A, y = C, colour = factor(B))) +
  ## add point geom with alpha set
  geom_point(alpha = 1/5) +
  ## title the legend "Custom Colours" and make the factor level 1 be blue
  ## and 2 be red
  scale_colour_manual("Custom Colours",
                      value = c("1" = "blue", "2" = "red"))
###################################

HTH,

Josh

messages.subject: Re: Colour one set of bars differently in a bar plot
messages.subject_clean: Colour one set of bars differently in a bar plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

If you can live with both bars in the Overall group being the same color, it's not too difficult. Here's one way. (BTW, thank you for presenting code and a picture of what you're after - it's very helpful. The data...meh. dput(dataframe) would have been ideal.)

Given your data is read in,

# Reorder the factor levels
maternity.score.long$id <- ordered(maternity.score.long$id, levels = c(
  'Overall', 'K/Mposhi', 'Kitwe', 'Katete', 'Nchelenge', 'Lusaka',
  'Mwinilunga', 'Livingstone', 'Sesheke'))

# Add indicators for Overall and 'not Overall' - the idea is to make two geom_bar()
# plots, one for Overall, to which we set a color, and another geom_bar() for the
# non-Overall data, using your previous code.

maternity.score.long <- transform(maternity.score.long,
      m1 = rep(c(rep(1, 8), 0), 2), m2 = 1 - rep(c(rep(1, 8), 0), 2) )

# Use ggplot() to combine the two plots as layers:

g <- ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id))
g + geom_bar(aes(y = m1 * value, fill = variable),
             stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +
    geom_bar(aes(y = m2 * value), fill = 'orange',
             stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +
    theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +

   scale_fill_manual("",values=c("powderblue","violet")) +

   geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                 label = format(maternity.score.long$value,
                          digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust=hjust),
                          colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +

   opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=-45, hjust=0),
        title="Density score 2008 & 2010")

Setting the fill color in the second call to geom_bar() simplifies matters immensely.

The problem with having different colors for the bars in the Overall group is that you need to map a variable for fill color. By doing that, you will by default be adding those colors to the legend, which you don't want, but you'd need another fill_scale_manual() call to assign yellow and orange to the values for that variable and set legend = FALSE correctly. If someone else wants to have a go at that, please do. I tried two scale_fill_manual() calls (no dice - the second one overwrites the first, as expected), and set up two individual plots in the hope I could 'add' them together - that didn't work, either. I thought the second idea might have a chance, actually; here's what I tried:

# Need the ordered factors as in the above code - don't forget :)

maternity.score.long <- transform(maternity.score.long,
      m1 = rep(c(rep(1, 8), 0), 2), m2 = 1 - rep(c(rep(1, 8), 0), 2),
      gp = rep(c('A', 'B'), each = 9))     # add a character var (could be a factor, too...)

# First plot without the Overall group:
g <- ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id, fill = variable))
g0 <- g + geom_bar(aes(y = m1 * value, fill = variable),
             stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +
    theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +

   scale_fill_manual("",values=c("powderblue","violet")) +

   geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                 label = format(maternity.score.long$value,
                          digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust=hjust),
                          colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +

   opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=-45, hjust=0),
        title="Density score 2008 & 2010")

# Second plot with the Overall group only:
h <- ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id, fill = gp))
h0 <- h +  geom_bar(aes(y = m2 * value),
             stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +
     scale_fill_manual("", values = c('yellow', 'orange'), legend = FALSE) +
     theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +
     geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                 label = format(maternity.score.long$value,
                          digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust=hjust),
                          colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +

     opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=-45, hjust=0),
        title="Density score 2008 & 2010")

# Superimpose?  Alas, no...
h0 + g0

If there's a way to pull this off, I'd love to see it.  Is rock star Hadley in the house?  :)  *

HTH,
Dennis

* If you don't get the reference, see  http://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/  and look for the article 'R is Hot: Part 3'. Sorry, Hadley, I couldn't resist :)

> That is precisely what I meant. The advantage of this format is that the

> variable and the class of the object will be the same on both ends. You've
> now made it much easier for others to participate in the quest of solving
> your problem :)

I thought I'd give it a crack as well.

My first thought was that the fill colour is controlled by the
interaction of the "variable" column and whether it is the overall
group (id=="Overall"), so why not set that explicitly.

[using the dput'd maternity.score.long and Dennis' ordering of the id
variable]

ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = value, fill = interaction(variable,id=="Overall")),

    stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +
  theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +
  scale_fill_manual("",

breaks=c("GF2008.FALSE","SAM2010.FALSE","GF2008.TRUE","SAM2010.TRUE"),
    values=c("powderblue","violet","yellow","orange"),
    labels=c("GM2008","SAM2001","","")) +

  geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                 label = format(maternity.score.long$value,
                          digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust=hjust),
                          colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=-45, hjust=0),
        title="Density score 2008 & 2010")

This is almost there, except there are entries in the legend for the
Overall bars (at least color boxes; the labels have been blanked
out).  I thought limits might help, but by limiting the scale to just
the non-overall groups, the overall group is dropped (as is consistent
for ggplot; data points outside the imposed limits of a scale are
dropped).  I don't know of any way to force a legend to only show
certain values rather than limit the data to them (somewhat analogous
to coord_cartesian(xlim=...) which limits what part of the x-axis is
shown, even though it does not limit the data used).

I got something to work, but it is VERY hackish, and I feel like I'm
subverting mechanisms rather than using them properly. In other words,
I can do it, but I won't say I'm proud of how I did it ;)

ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = value, fill = variable),
    data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id != "Overall",],

    stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +

  geom_bar(aes(x=as.numeric(id)-0.2, y = value, width=0.4),
    fill = 'yellow',
    data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id == "Overall" &
maternity.score.long$variable == "GF2008",],
    stat = 'identity') +
  geom_bar(aes(x=as.numeric(id)+0.2, y = value, width=0.4),
    fill = 'orange',
    data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id == "Overall" &
maternity.score.long$variable == "SAM2010",],
    stat = 'identity') +

  theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +
  scale_fill_manual("",values=c("powderblue","violet")) +
   geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                 label = format(maternity.score.long$value,
                          digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust=hjust),
                          colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +

width.  Also, I subset the data using the data argument rather than
multiplying by indicator variables like Dennis did.  Either way works
and is a matter of taste.  The yellow and orange bars might be a touch
narrower than the others (it's close but I can't quite tell); you can
adjust them by changing the offset in the ase(x=...) and the width
there as well.  The width should be twice the offset so that they will
touch.
