messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Kudos, Brian!! The first job is to get it right, then to make it beautiful. I appreciate the explanation of your thought process, too; it was very helpful. Subsetting the data was definitely better than my approach to the problem.

Just a couple of tweaks to the code to make it 'perfect'. I wouldn't have noticed that the Overall bars were thinner than the others until Brian mentioned it, so I played around using his advice, taking the space between bar pairs as the calibrator. I also wanted the numbers over the bars to be better centered, so I toyed with the hjust argument in geom_text(). The key was to start with hjust = 0.5 and think about how to increase the horizontal distance between labels.

Hopefully, this completes Marina's 'what_I_want' graph :)

ggplot(maternity.score.long, aes(x = id)) +
 geom_bar(aes(y = value, fill = variable),
   data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id != "Overall",],
   stat = 'identity', position = 'dodge', width = 0.6) +

 geom_bar(aes(x=as.numeric(id)-0.225, y = value, width=0.45),

   fill = 'yellow',
   data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id == "Overall" &
maternity.score.long$variable == "GF2008",],
   stat = 'identity') +

 geom_bar(aes(x=as.numeric(id)+0.225, y = value, width=0.45),

   fill = 'orange',
   data=maternity.score.long[maternity.score.long$id == "Overall" &
maternity.score.long$variable == "SAM2010",],
   stat = 'identity') +
 theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab('Score') + ylim(0, 100) +
 scale_fill_manual("",values=c("powderblue","violet")) +
  geom_text(aes(y = value + 0.2,
                label = format(maternity.score.long$value,

                         digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust = rep(c(1.25, -0.25), each = 9)),
#                         digits=1, nsmall=0), hjust= hjust),

                         colour="black", vjust=-0.4, size=3) +
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=-45, hjust=0),
       title="Density score 2008 & 2010")

Thanks to Marina for an interesting, well-posed problem. I learned a lot while working on it.

Cheers,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I would like to add the median for each "bl"-group per year...

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(234)
kr <- rep(paste(seq(1:3), seq(9:1), sep=""), 3)

v1 <- rep(100 * seq(0.1, 0.9, by=0.1), 3) * runif(27)
df <- data.frame(bl = substr(kr,1,1), kr, jahr, v1)

m <- ggplot(df, aes(x=jahr, y=v1,  group=kr))
m <- m + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~ bl)
m

dfmed <- ddply(df, .(bl, jahr), function(x) median(x$v1))

## This makes no sense...
m <- m + geom_line(data=dfmed, color="red")

Many thanks in advance for any help.
Patrick

hi, there are two points.
dfmed has V1, not v1, column.

or

will do that.

messages.subject: Re: Plotting a Scalar on a Circular Domain
messages.subject_clean: Plotting a Scalar on a Circular Domain
messages.body_plain:
Lorenzo

Here you go:

library(ggplot2)

radius <- 1
resolution <- 0.01
# construct grid

cgrid <- expand.grid(x=seq(-radius, radius, resolution), y=seq(-
radius, radius, resolution))
cgrid$incircle <- ((cgrid$x^2 + cgrid$y^2) <= radius^2)
cgrid <- cgrid[cgrid$incircle==TRUE, ]

# add colour

cgrid$colour <- abs(cos(cgrid$x/radius))
str(cgrid)

p <- ggplot(cgrid, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill=colour)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="red", high="blue")

print(p)

--

Andrie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel:

Try this - I separated the text labels into a separate data frame and used geom_text() instead. I may have gotten the coordinates wrong, but there are two labels per graph now.

Starting with your data frame df, create a new data frame that contains the coordinates, label and group ID.  grupo was stolen from df, so the order may be wrong.  I couldn't figure out why you had three text labels at x = 0.95 and one at x = 1.9 (pre-flip) so I'll let you sort that out.

plab <- data.frame(x = c(1.9, rep(0.95, 3)),
                   y = c(230, 500, 130, 130),
   lab = c('P = 0.02', 'P = 0.04', 'P = 0.15', 'P = 0.09'),

   grupo = c("Resultados Estadísticamente Significativo",
             "Resultados Estadísticamente Significativo",
             "Resultados Estadísticamente No Significativo",

             "Resultados Estadísticamente No Significativo"))
plab$lab <- as.character(plab$lab)    # convert labels to character

# Move aes terms from your object p into geom_pointrange(); otherwise there's a clash with geom_text() later.
p <- ggplot(df)
p + geom_pointrange(aes(y=b, x=a, ymin= li,
                    ymax= ls, colour = a), size = 0.8) +
     coord_flip() + theme_bw() + geom_hline(yintercept=0.0) +

     ylab("Diferencia en tamaño poblacional (Tamaño del Efecto)") +
     xlab("Estudio") + facet_wrap(~ grupo, scales = "free")  +

     geom_text(data = plab, aes(x = x, y = y, label = lab), size = 3) +

     opts(legend.position = "none") +
     scale_colour_manual(values = c("red","blue"))

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
HiL

Here's one way:

# Toy example
d <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + xlim(0, 10) + ylim(0, 10) +
    expand_limits(x = 0, y = 0)

This makes the axis origin (0, 0). If you want to get rid of the padding so that the axes are flush with the L of the plot region, you need to add the following:

    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

The first value in expand is the multiplicative expansion factor, the proportion of 'padding' between the edge of the plot region and the axis. The second value is an additive expansion parameter. This is mentioned in the help on scale_*_continuous(). The default is (0.05, 0), which means 5% padding around the perimeter and no additive expansion.

Warning: If you do this, the points on the edges of the plot will be partially clipped, which is why it's usually a better idea to make the first coordinate in expand > 0, perhaps 0.02 or more.

I always forget this, so as a reminder, expand is discussed in a paragraph on p. 99 of Hadley's book.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Last time I thought about this I convinced myself that one should
write a geom_raster for ggplot2. Unfortunately, I haven't found the
time / understanding required to write one. My lame attempt at
borrowing code from lattice::panel.levelplot.raster resulted in this,

library(ggplot2)

GeomRaster <- proto(Geom, {

  draw <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ..., interpolate=TRUE)
    {
      with(coordinates$transform(data, scales),
           {
           ux <- sort(unique(x[!is.na <http://is.na>(x)]))
           xwid <- mean(diff(ux))

           uy <- sort(unique(y[!is.na <http://is.na>(y)]))
           ywid <- mean(diff(uy))

           ncolumns <- length(ux)
           nrows <- length(uy)

           xlow <- ux[1] - 0.5 * xwid
           xhigh <- ux[ncolumns] + 0.5 * xwid

           ylow <- uy[1] - 0.5 * ywid
           yhigh <- uy[nrows] + 0.5 * ywid

           ## create a suitable matrix of colors
           zmat <- rep("transparent", ncolumns * nrows)
           idx <- match(x, ux)
           idy <- match(y, rev(uy)) # image goes top to bottom
           id <- idy + nrows * (idx-1L)

           zmat[id] <- fill

           dim(zmat) <- c(nrows, ncolumns)
           grid.raster(as.raster(zmat), interpolate = interpolate,
                       x = xlow, y = ylow,
                       width = xhigh - xlow, height = yhigh - ylow,
                       just = c("left", "bottom"),
                       default.units = "native")

           ggname(.$my_name(), rasterGrob(as.raster(zmat),
interpolate = interpolate,
                                          x = xlow, y = ylow,
                                          width = xhigh - xlow, height
= yhigh - ylow,
                                          just = c("left", "bottom"),
                                          default.units = "native", gp=gpar())
                  )})
    }

  objname <- "raster"

  default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour=NA, linetype=1, alpha = 1)
  required_aes <- c("x", "y", "fill")
  guide_geom <- function(.) "polygon"

  examples <- function(.) {
    ggplot(melt(volcano), aes(x=X1, y=X2, fill=value)) + geom_raster()
  }
}
)

geom_raster <- GeomRaster$build_accessor()

p <-
ggplot(melt(volcano), aes(x=X1, y=X2, fill=value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0))+
  scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0))

p +  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(20, 50), ylim=c(30,70))

For some reason this code fails when setting xlim or ylim.

Anyway, that may be a start. Should anyone wish to improve it, please
let me know.

baptiste

I don't know why it's so slow, but I suspect it's more to do with a
general ggplot2 behavior rather than this particular geom. Consider
this dummy example,

p = ggplot(melt(matrix(rnorm(1e6),1e3))) + geom_blank(aes(X1,X2))

messages.subject: histogram and density ..count..
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'd like to superimpose a histogram and a density plot, both using
..count.. as the y variable,

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(1e4, 10, 1))

foo <- function(n)
 ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..), binwidth=diff(range(d$x))/n,
                 fill="grey50", colour="grey40") +
  geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",
            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2) +
  scale_x_continuous("x") +
  scale_y_continuous("Count") +
  theme_bw()

foo(10) # density and histogram roughly of same height
foo(40) # histogram much below

My very naive understanding of histograms and density plots using
..count.. would have been that no matter the binwidth, the area under
the curve and the histogram should be similar. This isn't the case
here; should I adjust some parameters, or is this a bad idea
altogether?

Best regards,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: histogram and density ..count..
messages.body_plain:
Hi Baptiste:

On Mon, Oct 25, 2010 at 1:25 AM, baptiste auguie <bapt...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> Dear list,
>
> I'd like to superimpose a histogram and a density plot, both using
> ..count.. as the y variable,
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> d <- data.frame(x=rnorm(1e4, 10, 1))
>
> foo <- function(n)
>  ggplot(d, aes(x=x)) +
>  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..), binwidth=diff(range(d$x))/n,
>                 fill="grey50", colour="grey40") +
>  geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",
>            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2) +
>  scale_x_continuous("x") +
>  scale_y_continuous("Count") +
>  theme_bw()
>
> foo(10) # density and histogram roughly of same height
> foo(40) # histogram much below

If you plot a histogram on a density scale, it adjusts the heights so that the sum of the areas is 1. This is on the same scale as a density estimate, whose total area under the curve is 1. If you use the count scale, then multiplying the densities by the count should work in principle, but the problem is that the density doesn't adjust for the way that the histogram is binned, and that's what I think you're seeing. Finer partitions of the x-scale will reduce the counts in each bin, so the heights of the bars will get lower as the binwidths shrink. But AFAICT, there is no way to pass that information on to the density, so it should look the same no matter how the histograms are partitioned, since all you've done is to take the density estimate and blown it up by a factor of n.

Example:

x <- data.frame(x = rnorm(1000))
g <- ggplot(x, aes(x = x))

# Both histogram and density plot on density scale:

g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..) + geom_density()
g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..)) + geom_density()
g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), binwidth = 0.05) + geom_density()
g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), binwidth = 0.1) + geom_density()

# Both histogram and density plot on count scale:

g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..)) + geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",

            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2)

g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..), binwidth = 0.5) + geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",

            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2)

g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..), binwidth = 1.0) + geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",

            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2)

g + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..), binwidth = 0.1) + geom_line(aes(y = ..count..), stat="density",

            size = 1, colour="red", linetype=2)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I am recently new to using R within this year. I bought the book on
ggplot2 and have been loving the package a lot.
I have two questions regarding ggplot2.

The first is about graphing pictures. I used hadley's code in the book
for fortifying images that were loaded with the EBimage package.
I got ggplot2 to plot a nice picture of some microscopy images. What I
would like to do it to bind each image to a particular row of a
dataframe of conditions and then facet plot 4 to 8 images on one graph
in ggplot2. I have not been able to figure out a way to do this
without coercing each image into a dataframe and then rind them all
into one dataframe. This however is too much memory consumed and gives
many errors.
Is there is a way with the fortify method of plotting multiple
pictures faceted in ggplot2?

My second question is about facet_grid.
I have been using it to plot several factors of conditions on my data.
Such as the following:
facet_grid(Wash ~ Cell_Line + Butyrate)
the facet labels are not what I would expect
I get a set of facet labels that make no sense the column headers
should be 1st condition above the second condition Cell_Line over
Butyrate, but that is not what I get

Am I doing something wrong or does ggplot2 have a bug in it that
doesn’t work when facet_grid uses multiple items for either the row or
column facets?

Many Thanks

This is a known bug, I believe.  The plot should be correct, but the
labels will not be. See:
http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/labels/bug#issue/87

Here is one option as a way to circumvent the issue:

# Example using mtcars data
dat <- with(mtcars, data.frame(mpg, hp, cyl = factor(cyl),
            vs = factor(vs), am = factor(am),
            vsam = factor(paste(am, vs, sep = "\n"))))

library(ggplot2)
# using vs + am works, but incorrect labels
ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl ~ vs + am)
# using vsam, works with correct labels
ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) + geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl ~ vsam)

Cheers,

Josh

Hi:

What Brian casually failed to mention is that his novel use of scale_fill_manual() eliminated the need for three geom_bar() calls plus manual adjustment to the widths that was present in previous posts in this thread. This plot code is worth studying - the scale_fill_manual() trick is inspired. Great job, Brian - thanks for sharing!

Regards,
Dennis

If your mds is called mds and your data, data, then you can do something like:

pts <- mds$points
colnames(pts) <- paste("M", 1:ncol(pts), sep="")
ord <- cbind(data, pts)

and then plot ord.

Hadley

messages.subject: Left justification of axis text
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to make a dotplot. I have about 60 points, each with a longish descriptive label so I'd like to print the labels along the y-axis and plot the value along the x-axis. The problem comes when I want to left-justify the axis text as in the following example (with just two points).

test.dat <-
  data.frame(desc=c("A very long name", "Another very long name"),
             value=c(2,3))

qplot(x=value, y=desc, data=test.dat) +    opts(axis.text.y=theme_text(hjust=0))

When I do this, the labels are indeed left-justified but they start at the y-axis and so disappear under the graph. If I keep them right-justified (hjust=1, the default), I can see them fine but they are not as easy to read.

Is there a way of using axis.text.y so I can left-justify the labels starting far away enough from the axis that they can be seen? Or do I have to add a text geom, which would I assume would give me finer-grain control? Or is there some other way? Thanks.

I am using ggplot2 0.8.6 and R 2.10.1. Thanks.

 Jeff

On 10-10-27 10:58 AM, Peng Yu wrote:
> Hi,
>
> facet_grid doesn't add labels automatically. For example, I want 'drv'
> be added at the top and 'cyl' be added at the right. Since the labels

> qplot(displ, hwy, data=mpg) + facet_grid(drv ~ cyl)
>
>

  One possibility, from
<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2403466/greek-letters-in-ggplot-strip-text>,
is:

label_parseall <- function(variable, value) {
    plyr::llply(value, function(x) parse(text = paste(variable,
        x, sep = "==")))

}
> qplot(displ, hwy, data=mpg) + facet_grid(drv ~

cyl,labeller=label_parseall)

 [ label_parseall() is actually overkill for this problem, it's
intended for when there is Greek/math annotation in the labels]

  I can see that one might want the labels to be generated a single
time, in the outer margin, but how would one then distinguish them from
the axis labels?  I suppose if they were in 'outer gray strips' ...

  Ben Bolker

Hi Peng,

You are looking for stat = "identity".  For example:

# Some data
dat <- data.frame(Group = c("A", "B", "C"),
                  height = c(50, 60, 70))

# A bar plot
ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = Group, y = height)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")

# Also note that no information is lost if you do

ggplot(data = dat, aes(x = Group, y = height)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + scale_y_continuous(lim = c(0, 70))

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: Controlling axes without data loss
messages.body_plain:
I want a bubble plot of mean length of stay (LOS_mean) by readmission
rate (RR_mean). Each data point is a hospital, and is weighted by the
number of patients seen (RR_N). There are some outliers in the data. A
few hospitals have RR_mean=1 or 0. These hospitals generally have very
few observations (RR_N as small as 1). If I create a subset, with the
restriction RR_N>=100, and plot thusly:

> facility_sub<-subset(facility, RR_N>=100)

> ggplot(facility_sub, aes(LOS_mean, RR_mean, weight=RR_N, size=RR_N)) +
>  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=T) +
>  opts(legend.position = "none") +
>  labs(x="Mean Length of Stay", y="Readmission Rate")

I get (almost; see ** below) the exact plot I would like. However, the
LS fit line and SE are based on the subsetted data. I would like them
to be based on all observations, but to have the window 'zoomed in' on
this portion of the plot. As I undertand it, using the subset (like I
did above) is equivalent to using scale_x/y_continuous() (i.e. throws
out data points that aren't within my limits).

If I plot using the full dataset and utilize coord_cartesian():

> ggplot(facility, aes(LOS_mean, RR_mean, weight=RR_N, size=RR_N)) +
>  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=T) +
>  opts(legend.position = "none") +
>  labs(x="Mean Length of Stay", y="Readmission Rate") +
>  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(,10),ylim=c(.03,.19))

 I do get a zoomed in view of the data, and the LS fit line and SE are
based on the full data, BUT the y-axis labelling has disappeared and
the backgroud grid squares are now much larger than before. It is
literally like 'looking at the plot under a magnifying glass', to
reference the book. I would like to maintain the look of the first
plot (same axes and axes labels, same grid size in background, etc),
but display the geom_smooth of the full dataset.

Any suggestions? Thanks in advance, Skyler

** I said the first plot gave me *almost* exactly what I wanted
visually. The only complaint was the legend. I decided to just remove
it. The issue I was having is that both the geom_point and geom_smooth
were being forced in the same legend. That is, the legend showed the
weighting used (i.e. a hospital with N observations has a dot 'this
big'), but then on top of the displayed dot, was a big blue line (from
the geom_smooth). I can plot the geom_smooth first, then geom_point,
but this just moves the blue swaths to the background in the legend
(slightly better looking, but still less than ideal), and did the same
in the plot (the line was covered by the data points. I don't want
that to happen). So, essentially, is there a way to have the legend
represent only the geom_point, and NOT the geom_smooth?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
In the future, taking the time to make a simpler example will likely
result in more (and faster) responses. That said, I took some time to
look through your code and came to the following conclusions

1) Your approach will work provided that you create colours as a named
vector. That is, you defined colours as

colours <- c("Control-Region" <- "lightblue4", "tRNA" <- "magenta4",
"rRNA" <- "mediumaquamarine", "Non-Coding" <- "sienna4", "ND1" <-
"magenta", "ND2" <- "mediumblue", "CO1" <- "olivedrab", "CO2" <-
"orange2", "ATP8" <- "orchid4", "ATP6" <- "red3", "CO3" <-
"royalblue2", "ND3" <- "palegreen4", "ND4L" <- "grey0", "ND4" <-
"pink4", "ND5" <- "yellow4", "ND6" <- "steelblue4", "CYB" <-
"tan","red")

when you should have defined it as

colours = c("Control-Region" = "lightblue4", "tRNA" = "magenta4",
"rRNA" = "mediumaquamarine", "Non-Coding" = "sienna4", "ND1" =
"magenta", "ND2" = "mediumblue", "CO1" = "olivedrab", "CO2" =
"orange2", "ATP8" = "orchid4", "ATP6" = "red3", "CO3" =
"royalblue2", "ND3" = "palegreen4", "ND4L" = "grey0", "ND4" =
"pink4", "ND5" = "yellow4", "ND6" = "steelblue4", "CYB" =
"tan","red")

2) You are working too hard. You can achieve the same result by
changing gene to a factor (in both lines and mitodata) and getting rid
of the scale_colour_manual part (you also need to set the constant
line colors outside of the aes() calls to prevent them from inclusion
in the legend).

Best,
Ista

  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(2.8,10.2),ylim=c(.03,.19)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(.05, .2, by=.025)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(3, 10, by=1))

-Ista

Ista Zahn-

1. You definitey fixed my legend issue. I was unaware of the 'legend='
argument. This isn't in the book, nor the R help (?geom_smooth), nor
the online help <http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_smooth.html>. Is there
another source where I could have found it?

2. I'm 99.9% sure you fixed the axes issue, but just to be explicit:
Using "scale_x_continuous(limits=)" throws out any data not included
in the specified limits (I don't want that to happen); whereas using
"scale_x_continuous(breaks=)" calculates statistics (i.e. the LS fit
line and SE) using all the data, but only displays data contained in
the range of the 'breaks'. True?

Thank you very much.

messages.subject: Re: plot with error-bars and upperlimits
messages.body_plain:
On Oct 27, 9:07 am, ashish <mahabal.ash...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I started using ggplot recently and find it amazing.
>
> I have a table with x, y, y-error.
> I wish to plot the points with error-bars on y, except that if the y-
> error equals a fixed large value (say 99.0) I want to show it as an
> upper-limit (using another color or symbol for that row, or a one

> sided error-bar). An example is shown at this URL:http://nesssi.cacr.caltech.edu/catalina/20101019/1010190150134113452p...

>
> If I have the following snippet of a table, how do I do it with
> ggplot2?
>
> 2454938.875    21.27    99.00
> 2454938.887    20.05     0.15
> 2454938.898    20.20     0.18
> 2454938.909    21.11    99.00
> 2454938.922    21.01    99.00
> 2454938.932    21.07    99.00
> 2454938.945    20.68      0.24
>
> Here is what I do up to the error-part bit:
>
> X <- read.table('mydata')
> qplot(V1,V2,data=X,ylim=c(max(X$V2),min(X$V2))) +
> geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=V2+V3,ymax=V2-V3),width=0.1)
>
> or
>
> qplot(V1,V2,data=X) + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(max(X$V2),min(X$V2))) +
> geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=V2-V3,ymax=V2+V3))

Create an indicator variable for which type of plotting you want, and
then subset the data on that variable for each plot type, At the same
time, use that variable in the colour and shape aesthetic.  I manually
set the colors and hid the legends.  Setting the ymax to Inf will draw
out to the extreme of the graph without extending the scale.
scale_y_reverse inverts the axis (without having to know the limits).

X <-
structure(list(V1 = c(2454938.875, 2454938.887, 2454938.898,
2454938.909, 2454938.922, 2454938.932, 2454938.945), V2 = c(21.27,
20.05, 20.2, 21.11, 21.01, 21.07, 20.68), V3 = c(99, 0.15, 0.18,
99, 99, 99, 0.24)), .Names = c("V1", "V2", "V3"), class =
"data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-7L))

X <- transform(X, limit=(V3==99))

ggplot(X, aes(x=V1, y=V2, colour=limit, shape=limit)) +
geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=V2+V3,ymax=V2-V3),width=0.1, data=X[!X$limit,])
+
geom_point(data=X[!X$limit,]) +
geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=V2, ymax=Inf), data=X[X$limit,]) +
scale_y_reverse() +
scale_colour_manual(values=c("blue","red"), legend=FALSE) +
scale_shape(legend=FALSE)

> BTW, is there any better way to invert the y-axis than what I am
> doing? My first method will tend to not plot the error bars on the two
> extreme points in y.

That's because using ylim tells ggplot to throw out any points/data
outside that range, so the upper error bars get tossed out.

> Thanks!
> -ashish

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

# An example of my data
set.seed(1716)

                      variable = factor(rep(c(0:1), 50)),
                      value = sample(0:4, 100, replace = TRUE))

# individual lines, works fine
ggplot(data = sampdat, aes(x = variable, y = value, group = ids)) +
  geom_line()

messages.subject: Re: Overall trendline
messages.body_plain:
Hi Josh:

I think the problem is that group = 1 is meant to be used for a double purpose here. In the book example of a spaghetti plot (sec. 4.9.3), geom_smooth(aes(group = 1)) was applied to a continuous x variable and rendered an overall mean + SE envelope of the individual profiles. When the x-variable is a factor, one uses geom_line(aes(group = 1)) to plot a line across the levels of that factor. You're apparently trying to do both in one call, and evidently ggplot() is balking :)

On Wed, Oct 27, 2010 at 5:39 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi All,
>
> I am sure I am missing something very obvious, but I've been going in circles trying to figure out why this does not work.  I have some (discrete) data, that was measured at T1 and T2.  I want to plot all the individual lines (a la a spaghetti plot), and then add an overall line of best fit.  This sample data illustrates my problem and is fairly representative of my actual data.
>
> # An example of my data
> set.seed(1716)
> sampdat <- data.frame(ids = rep(1:50, each = 2),
>                      variable = factor(rep(c(0:1), 50)),
>                      value = sample(0:4, 100, replace = TRUE))
>
> # individual lines, works fine
> ggplot(data = sampdat, aes(x = variable, y = value, group = ids)) +
>  geom_line()
>
> # How I *thought* I should add the overall trend line
> ggplot(data = sampdat, aes(x = variable, y = value, group = ids)) +
>  geom_line() + stat_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", size = 2, colour = "blue")

How about something like this?

# Get mean/SD summaries from each level of variable:
dsumm <- ddply(sampdat, .(variable), summarise, m = mean(value), s = sd(value))

# Spaghetti plots
g <- ggplot(data = sampdat, aes(x = variable)) +
      geom_line(aes(y = value, group = ids))

# Mean line with geom_ribbon to add SDs
g + geom_line(data = dsumm, aes(y = m, group = 1), color = 'blue', size = 1) +
     geom_ribbon(data = dsumm, aes(ymin = m - s, ymax = m + s, group = 1),
                   colour = 'gray80', alpha = I(0.2))

Not perfect, but perhaps enough to get you started.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: New to ggplot2 and question
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The key insight that will help you with these issues is that
properties in ggplot2 can be set in one of two ways: to fixed values,
or mapped to variables. To map a property (such as size, shape, color,
position, etc) to a variable, you set the mapping inside an aes()
call. To set a property to a fixed value, you set it outside the aes()
call. Here is an example

library(ggplot2)

## make up some data (this is an important step!)

td <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), y=rnorm(100), a=rep(c("a", "b"), 50),
b=rep(c("a", "b"), each=50))

## create the base plot similar to yours (I could not reproduce yours
becase I lack the data)

figura <- ggplot(data=td, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
facet_grid(facets=~a)
figura <- figura + geom_smooth(aes(linetype=b))

## print the plot setting size to a fixed value.

figura + geom_point(aes(shape=b), size=1)
figura + geom_point(aes(shape=b), size=2)
figura + geom_point(aes(shape=b), size=5)

## print the plot setting size to a variable
figura + geom_point(aes(size=b))
## If you want to change the values used when a property is mapped to
a variable, then you can use scale_*_ manual. For example

figura + geom_point(aes(size=b)) + scale_size_manual(values=c(1,2))
figura + geom_point(aes(size=b)) + scale_size_manual(values=c(3,6))

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: question on "coord_polar()"
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I recently started to use "ggplot2" and really enjoy using it.

I recently observed some weird cases while using "ggplot2".
When I try to draw pie chart using "coord_polar()",
the resulting pie chart has dent in some cases.

Please see the linked picture below.

http://picasaweb.google.com/dongjun.chung/DropBox#5533176768915174338

However, if I round the values, then such dent goes away
(it took some time to figure this out after lots of trials & errors).
This behavior was somewhat unexpected to me.
Does any one have similar experiences?
Is rounding values the only way to fix this problem?
And can someone explain to me why this happens?

----------------------------------------

library(ggplot2)
piedata <- data.frame(
    c( 0.1159132, 21.7254512, 0.1987084, 55.5224375, 0.0496771,
22.3878126,

25.0970246 ),
    rep( c('A','B','C','D','E','F'),2 ), rep( c('A','B'), each=6 ) )
colnames(piedata) <- c("Ratio","Category","Set")

p <- ggplot( data=piedata, aes( x=factor(1), y=Ratio,
fill=Category ) )
p <- p + geom_bar( width=1 )
p <- p + facet_grid( facets=. ~ Set )
p <- p + coord_polar( theta="y" )
p

----------------------------------------

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: question on "coord_polar()"
messages.body_plain:
hi

probably this is because coord-polar calculates the distance between
vertices using Euclidean data and polar coordinate.
an easy hack is like this:

CoordPolar$distance <- function(., x, y, details) {
    max_dist <- dist_polar(details$r.range, details$theta.range)
    if (.$theta == "x") {
      d <- .$transform(data.frame(theta=x, r=y), details)
      dist_polar(theta = d$theta, r = d$r) / max_dist
    } else {
      d <- .$transform(data.frame(theta=y, r=x), details)
      dist_polar(r = d$r, theta = d$theta) / max_dist
    }
  }

messages.subject: Re: axis.title.x = theme_blank() not working
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it was coord_flip(), I think it was theme_bw() which has defaults for axis.x.text that are black. When you set your axis text with opts to theme_blank() and then had the call for theme_bw() afterwards it uses the last call to set the theme. At least that's my experience. Like you said Ista, putting your opts() call at the end fixes it.

B

On Thu, Oct 28, 2010 at 17:39, Ista Zahn <iz...@psych.rochester.edu> wrote:
> Hi Manuel,
>
> On Thu, Oct 28, 2010 at 11:52 AM, Manuel Spínola <mspin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear list members,
> >
> > I am trying to put 2 different plots in one page (p1 and p2):
> >
> > a= rnorm(20, 5.35, 1.6)
> > b = rnorm(20, 3.5, 1.1)
> > grupo = rep(c("a", "b"), c(20, 20))
> > cont = c(a,b)
> > cont
> > df = data.frame(cont, grupo)
> >
> > sea = sd(a)/sqrt(20)
> > seb = sd(b)/sqrt(20)
> >
> > dfplot = data.frame(sexo = factor(c("Machos", "Hembras"), levels=c("Machos",
> > "Hembras")),
> >  punto = c(mean(a), mean(b)),
> >  ymin = c(mean(a) - 2*sea, c(mean(b) - 2*sea)),
> >  ymax = c(mean(a) + 2*seb, c(mean(b) + 2*sea)))
> > dfplot
> >
> > pa = ggplot(dfplot, aes(x = sexo, y = punto, ymin= ymin, ymax= ymax, colour
> > = sexo))
> > p1 = pa + geom_pointrange(size = 0.8) + xlab("Sexo") + ylab("Concentración
> > contaminante (ppm)") + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,6)) + theme_bw() +
> > opts(legend.position = "none")

> > dfdif = data.frame(

> >    punto = 1.72,
> >    ymin = 1.06,
> >    ymax = 2.39)
> >
> > pb = ggplot(dfdif, aes(x = dif, y = punto, ymin= ymin, ymax= ymax, colour =
> > "red"))
> > p2 = pb + geom_pointrange(size = 0.8) + opts(axis.title.x = theme_blank()) +

> > coord_flip()  + ylab("Diferencia entre machos y hembras (ppm)") + theme_bw()

messages.subject: grid.clip and ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Although is a subject from a year ago, I am facing may be a similar

one but I am unable to solve it.

Basically I am unable to clip subplots to their specific viewports

within a grid.layout. Specifically if I use highly negative values in

plot.margin (I do it to join successive plots) for a particular side

of a subplot it invades the nearby viewport and hide it if it is in

it's left side.

Does some know if this is a misunderstanding from my side of using

plot.margin with viewports or is it due to the clip option which is by

default "inherit"

I tried to change the default clip argument to "on" but without

success. Is there anyway to fix it?

For grid.layout I used a code from Learning R web page, something like

the following (where I tried clip="on" on both viewport functions)

Layout <- grid.layout(nrow = 3, ncol = 2, widths = unit(c(1, 1),

c("null", "null")), heights = unit(c(1, 1, 1), c("null", "null",

"lines")))

grid.show.layout(Layout)

vplayout <- function(...) { grid.newpage()

pushViewport(viewport(layout = Layout, clip="on"))

}

subplot <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col

= y, clip="on")

Fig <- function(a, b, c, d) { vplayout()

print(a, vp=subplot(1,1))

print(b, vp=subplot(1,2))

print(c, vp=subplot(2,1))

print(d, vp=subplot(2,2))

grid.text("Days after anthesis", gp=gpar(fontsize=10), vp=subplot(3,

1:2))

}

Fig(t06, t07, rh06, rh07)

Thanks for your help
Afif

messages.subject: Re: grid.clip and ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think it's a limitation of Grid's clipping mechanism; AFAIK you
cannot clip a grob that contains new viewports.
That being said, I'm not sure why you should need negative margins?

library(gridExtra)
my.opts = opts(plot.margin=unit(c(0,-0.5,0,-0.5),"lines"),
axis.title.y=theme_blank(), axis.text.y=theme_blank() )
lp = replicate(4,qplot(1,1)  + my.opts,simplify=F)
do.call(grid.arrange, c(lp, sub="Days after anthesis"))

HTH,

baptiste

Bob

no_margins <- opts(
 axis.line =         theme_blank(),

 panel.background =  theme_blank(),

 panel.grid.major =  theme_blank(),
 panel.grid.minor =  theme_blank(),
 plot.background =   theme_blank(),
 plot.title =        theme_blank(),

)
ggplot(data=TinylandDF)+
  geom_polygon( aes(long, lat,

  geom_text( aes(labptX, labptY, label=region) ) +
  scale_fill_continuous(low = "grey80", high = "grey20") +
  coord_equal() +
  opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),

Hi Scott,
<rant> If you had provided us with the data your code uses it would
have increased it's value considerably. By not providing the data you
force your potential helpers to either respond abstractly and/or
without testing their solutions, or to make up a reproducible example
of their own. Please include code to generate an example data set, or
use dput() to include the actual data you are using. </rant>

OK now that that is out of my system, the answer to your question is
that you need to put the vline data in a separate data.frame. Here is
an example

dat <- data.frame(x=rnorm(20), y=rnorm(20), z=rep(c("a", "b"), each=10))

vline.dat <- data.frame(z=levels(dat$z), vl=c(0,1))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=vl), data=vline.dat) +
  facet_grid(.~z)

Best,
Ista
